subtopic: WESTERN ARCTIC (INUVIALUIT) CLAIMS SETTLEMENT ACT MEASURE TO AMEND-CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, of course if the Official Opposition concur in this motion. I just want to indicate to the House that the substance of this Bill has already been fully considered. We dealt with it in all stages at an earlier time.
The agreement between the Government of Canada and the Western Arctic Inuvialuit represents an important step forward in settling claims. The changes that we passed earlier were primarily of a technical nature. When we did so, no one picked up the fact that there was an error in the drafting of the legislation with respect to the date. That is what we are now correcting. It causes no problems at all.
However, I think we owe a debt of gratitude to the Senate for having detected this error. It is not a serious one, but there have been other occasions when bad drafting has led to some very serious repercussions.
I would simply draw to Your Honour's attention a piece of legislation called Bill C-31 wherein bad drafting resulted in a regulation now used by the Department of Indian Affairs to prohibit a significant number of people from applying for the reinstatement of their Indian status. This is what we now refer to as the infamous death rule. The Department of Justice looked at the statute and discovered that there was a difficulty
June 2, 1988

with it. Because there was a difficulty, it is now being applied in practice and affecting people's lives.
1 simply want to draw to the attention of the House and to the attention of the country that we around here can sometimes be a little too lax in legislative committees and, in certain cases, in standing committees, or if we are dealing with matters in Committee of the Whole. We need a kind of expertise so that these errors in drafting will not get away from us.
I just want to repeat that we cannot take it for granted that we can proceed on the basis of good faith that those who draft legislation for us always do it right. That is why we have to be continually vigilant.
I repeat that with this case it is not a serious error. It is just a small one. We can deal with it very easily. That, of course, is the intention of the Official Opposition.

subtopic: WESTERN ARCTIC (INUVIALUIT) CLAIMS SETTLEMENT ACT MEASURE TO AMEND-CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is nice to have an opportunity to speak for a moment to the amendment to Bill C-102. I spoke to senior people in the Department who are aware of how this came to be on page 2 in the first clause at line 13. The date, April 11, 1987, happened to be put in there. The actual document was typed with that date, as I understand it, at the top of the page, and the actual date of signature was put in, in ink, at the bottom of the page. When the draftspeo-ple were putting in a date, they in fact used the most visible and obvious typed date rather than the appropriate one, which is May 11, 1987.
I am assured that this is simply a technical change that resulted from a small error. It is not some other agreement or whatever, although I know that many first citizens in the country are deeply suspicious of what the federal Government does most of the time, if not all the time. They have every right to be given the assurance that it is not a change in any other way than to put the proper date on the document.
I want to remind Hon. Members about how long it has taken for us actually to get this done. The Inuvialuit, or as their negotiating arm was known, COPE, entered into the agreement with Canada on June 5, 1984. It was tabled in the House on June 19, 1984. It was passed by the House on June 26. That is almost four years to the day that the agreement was put in place. It has taken us four years of procedure to get to where we are today. It can go very quickly to get Royal Assent in order that, perhaps, it could be fully implemented by next week.
The Inuvialuit final agreement contained 18 principal points: 35,000 square miles in title fee simple absolute, full subsurface rights to 5,000 square miles, to roughly a seventh of the land, and on the other 30,000 square miles the Crown holds the rights to certain minerals, natural gas, oil, and so on.
The compensation was arranged at $44 million in 1977 dollars. Approximately $12 million was borrowed by the
Western Arctic (Inuvialuit) Claims Settlement Act
Inuvialuit and their negotiators to complete the process of negotiations. At present, the full amount in inflation protected dollars is $152 million, of which $73 million has been put out and there is approximately $73 million permitted yet outstanding.
I am pleased it is passing through this place today because the enrolment procedures for the Inuvialuit are being held up. They had planned to complete that this month. If the Governor General moves quickly, hopefully they may be able to complete that this month, or certainly by next month. I am pleased that after only four years of delay both Chambers have managed to patch things up and get the deal concluded.

speakeroldname: Mr. Stan Schellenberger (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to speak to this Bill, one which is being presented for second reading today. Hopefully, by agreement, it can move through the House today by way of Committee of the Whole and third reading. We wish to do this because of the significance of the Bill.
It has been brought forward by the Indian people. We are looking for an amendment at their request. This Bill was given extra direction at the conference held in the City of Edmonton where the Assembly of First Nations met and passed a resolution supporting this legislation. The band that initiated the Bill that we are discussing is the Kamloops Band of British Columbia. They began the process in January, 1985.
By the end of that year, well over 100 other bands from across the country had formally communicated their support of this legislation to the Government. In July, 1986, the General Assembly of First Nations endorsed the Kamloops proposal, as they did again in the last couple of days.
On March 16, 1988, the Confederacy of Nations of the Assembly of First Nations examined Bill C-115 itself and endorsed it in principle. The Assembly of First Nations requested only one small amendment to the text of the Bill, and this is included in the motions that have been prepared.
I also wish to speak to the opposition critics on four very minor amendments that must be proposed to this legislation, and we hope to do that in Committee of the Whole. Those amendments are prepared and hopefully will be endorsed by all of us.
Over the last several years Chief Clarence Jules of the Kamloops Band, when we should commend for his diligence and hard work in this area, has travelled extensively throughout the country explaining this proposal at countless meetings to any band or organization that wishes to listen. He has also been very diligent in his work on Parliament Hill with those of us who are interested in Indian matters. Indian people
understood what he was proposing and they supported him. I hope we will also do so today.
Chief Jules' attitude is one I share: as long as the Indian Act is with us, until such time as it is superseded by a higher and better law, then we should make the Act work for Indian people and not against them. Whatever gains we make in this way can be retained for the future in other legal expressions yet to come.
There are two main purposes to this Bill: first, to clarify the legal status of Indian lands; second, to establish the legal foundation for property taxation by band councils. These two purposes are closely related. I do not need to remind the House that land is one of the most vital and sacred concerns of Indian people. The lands that are set aside for Indian people must be under Indian control, and they must be legally disposed of in such a way as to provide maximum control and economic benefit to Indian communities.
One of the principal means by which Indian bands can benefit economically from their land is through leasing, both to Indians and in many cases to non-Indians, until such time as they have sufficient control, whether it is in farming, timber, or mining, to take over those apparatus themselves. The lease makes possible modern financial and contractual arrangements. Some bands may not wish to use their land in these ways, and that is their choice, but many bands wish to use their land base as a source of wealth and employment for their community, as well as underpinning their economic development. They must have that opportunity.
The great advantage to leasing arrangements is that the ultimate Indian interest in the land can be retained and the land is not lost from the reserve. At the same time, the lease provides the legal basis for the economic use of the land.
In order for bands to lease their land, the Indian Act requires that the land must first be surrendered to the Crown, which is then authorized to enter into the lease on behalf of the band. This is obviously an indirect and very complicated process. However, it has historical roots which touch on the basic nature of the relationship among the Crown, Indian land, and Indian people.
In this proposal to amend the Indian Act, Indian people have not asked that the surrender process be changed or removed. Such a step may come in the future, but only after much consideration has been given to the consequences for the Indian-Crown relationship. However, within the present context of the surrender process, the fundamental difference needs to be clarified between an absolute surrender of land for sale and a surrender for lease. At present this difference is merely mentioned in one line of the Indian Act. It is not clearly set out nor worked through the relevant sections of the Act.
June 2, 1988

The Bill before us will establish that a surrender may take one of two forms-first, an absolute surrender for sale which would remove land completely of all Indian interests and take it out of reserve, which is extremely rare, and, second, a surrender for lease or some other restricted purpose, in which case the land remains part of the reserve. Setting aside part of a reserve for leasing is not a surrender, nor is it a release of the Indian interest in the land.
In order to facilitate and strengthen the distinction between these two types of surrender, land surrendered for lease would be termed "designated land" and the process of such nonabsolute surrender would be termed "designation". This terminology is obviously far superior to the word "surrender", and the symbolic importance of this change is of great value.
As a result of these amendments Indian communities will be able to set land aside for development without fear of losing the Indian status of the land. The rights they obtain through the Indian Act will continue to apply, such as voting rights in band elections, protection of cultural property, and the power to govern the land through by-laws.
The last point is very important. At present it is not at all clear in the Indian Act whether the word "reserve" includes surrendered land of any type. There is, therefore, a risk that when land is surrendered for lease it might cease to be defined as part of the reserve and the by-law powers of the band council could not govern the land. This is a totally unacceptable loss of Indian jurisdiction and control of Indian land. It would also mean a very serious vacuum of local jurisdiction over leased Indian land. This has taken place in many instances across Canada and is why the band at Kamloops requested the change. This situation cannot be permitted to continue.
One of the most important by-law powers that bands need is their power to tax use of the land. That brings me to the second purpose of these amendments, which is to establish clearly that band councils have the power to tax any interest or use of reserve lands in order to defray their costs as the government of that land. Such taxation power is obviously indispensable to any form of modern government. Some bands may not wish to use this power, but it must be there for bands which wish to exercise it.
In fact, Section 83 of the Indian Act has provided a taxation power for band councils since 1951. It is possible, however, that the power might apply only to Indians. It may not, as presently worded, apply to non-Indian leaseholders. The amendments will make certain that non-Indians are covered.
Section 83 is being brought up to date in other ways as well. Bands will no longer need to be declared to have reached an advanced stage of development before they may pass money by-laws. This provision is offensive and pointless.
The enforcement powers of band councils needed for their tax systems will be strengthened. Band taxation by-laws will be required to include appeal procedures to ensure equity for
Indian Act
taxpayers. A general federal regulatory power is provided. Although no regulations are proposed at this time, the purpose of any future regulations would be to minimize ministerial discretion in respect of the exercise of band powers. If rules are necessary, they should be explicit and objective.
There is one final aspect of the Bill which I want to touch on in these remarks. There are certain sections of the Indian Act which create exclusively Indian land holdings in a reserve in which non-Indians cannot participate. The word "reserve" cannot include "designated land" for the purposes of the sections, since designated land is designed to include nonIndian participation. These sections are enumerated in the new definition of reserve, but Section 89 of the Act creates a special consideration in this context.
Section 89 protects Indian real and personal property on a reserve from any form of seizure or mortgage. It is a mixed blessing for Indian people. On one hand it protects their property, but on the other hand it prevents them from offering security for loans.
The question arises on how the concept of designated land should apply to Section 89. After all, the purpose of designated land is to allow leasehold interests to enter the legal and economic mainstream while protecting the underlying Indian interest in the land.
With this in mind, Section 89 is proposed for amendments so that leasehold interests in designated land would be made mortgageable. This will mean that an Indian person holding a lease on designated land would be able, just as a non-Indian is, to use the lease as security for a loan. There would be no risk to the ultimate reserve status of the land nor any possible loss of the ultimate Indian interest. Only the lease would be at risk. Of course, such leasehold interests would also remain under band council jurisdiction. This change should be a major breakthrough for the Indian economic use and benefit of reserve land.
The tendency in arguing for amendments to the Indian Act is either to do away with it entirely or to amend every section. Neither option is proposed here. Indian people have suggested a limited change to the Act. I believe these amendments are necessary and extremely helpful to Indian aspirations at this time, and I am pleased to be able to bring them to this House.
I want to add in closing that in August of 1987 the Department released an information booklet explaining these proposed amendments in detail. Over 6,000 copies of that booklet were distributed, including two separate mailings to all chiefs. Members of the House and the Senate were also sent copies, as were all provincial Governments and major associations of municipalities. These amendments have been developed in a very open process. Indeed, the content of this legislation has been developed in close consultation with Chief Jules, its main proponent from the Indian community.
I think the way in which this process has been undertaken shows that government and Indian co-operation on legislative

June 2, 1988
Indian Act
change is possible and can produce substantial and positive results. I hope we will see much more of that type of cooperation as we continue to make changes in the years ahead.
In conclusion, it is very important that we continue this kind of process to encourage the self-government movement toward which many of us in this House have worked so hard. This is one small change in that direction.

Nations' right to their lands and the waters and resources on those lands.
Bill C-l 15 has to be seen as part of the ancien regime, a part of the old order. You may remember from your history classes, Mr. Speaker, about the ancien regime in France prior to the French Revolution. At that time, it was necessary for a local congregation to come to the Estates General to get permission to repair the roof of the church. Bill C-l 15 is not very much different from that. We are participating in an action under the old order, an old order that simply must change in time.
It is regrettable and unfortunate that it is still necessary for Parliament to give First Nations the permission to tax nonIndian interests on their own lands, on lands they have designated for development or leasing. In the process of so doing we also have to make it clear, are the legislation does, that tax exemptions on purchases and incomes made on these lands are applicable as they are on so-called reserves.
It has become customary, when we amend the Indian Act, to go through some manner of consultation. The Parliamentary Secretary made it clear that there had been a consultation process, and in this case it has been a satisfactory one. The Assembly of First Nations, in 1986, adopted a resolution endorsing the position taken by Chief Manny Jules of the Kamloops Band. However, at the same time, I think this House ought to be aware that the Assembly of First Nations and other native organizations in Canada remain highly critical of this Government's reluctance to move forward with more vigour in the recognition of aboriginal self-governments.
I have to tell my colleagues in the House once again how distressed I am that the important work done a number of years ago by the Special Committee on Indian Self-Government in Canada has resulted in very little that is positive. I regret that the Department of Indian Affairs has chosen to use much of the vocabulary of this report but to go on denying the essence and the reality of what was recommended in that document.
In Indian-Government relations in Canada, there has been much betrayal by successive Governments, both federal and provincial. Since there is such a long record of broken promises, there remains a deep concern that revenue that will be raised on these conditionally surrendered lands, these designated lands, will in future offer the Government a reason for reducing the normal or regular financial support for band administration, for economic development, for housing, and for other ongoing programs which in reality constitute a part of the federal Government's obligations under treaty or other aboriginal rights.
I hope that will not happen. I hope that the Government will not tell a band that raises revenue in this manner that now that it has some money from its own lands it does not need the other programs and that it will give them to someone else.
That approach has been tried as a result of the settlement with the James Bay Cree. It was done with one particular band
Indian Act
in the southern part of the Province of Alberta, a band which received compensation from the Government for a cattle claim. When those moneys were disbursed, immediately the Government sought to reduce social assistance to the members of that band. That is the kind of betrayal that Indian people are concerned about. I want to make it clear that we will be watching carefully to see that, as a result of Bill C-l 15, this does not occur again.
Meanwhile, Chief Jules has made it clear that nothing in Bill C-l 15 will cause Indian bands to lose any jurisdiction on leased reserve lands, on these designated lands.
I conclude simply by saying that because the days of this Parliament are obviously and rapidly drawing to a close, Chief Jules wants to see this Bill become law and not die on the Order Paper. As the spokesperson for Indian and aboriginal affairs for the Liberal Party of Canada, I want to assure the chief of our complete support for and co-operation in dealing with this Bill. That is why the Parliamentary Secretary, the Minister, my colleague from the New Democratic Party, and I have agreed that when the Minister returns this afternoon we will deal with all remaining stages of this Bill, so that before this Parliament comes to an end Chief Manny Jules will have the legislation he so desperately wants, the legislation he worked so hard to attain.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to participate in the debate today, and I guess we can call it this afternoon now. I know that so long as the cable system in Edmonton, your hometown, Mr. Speaker, is still working, Manny will be watching with great interest this afternoon.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I would like the Hon. Member to know that they were watching at 12.30 this morning, and we are back again 12 hours later. I am sure they will be watching you also.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I know that sometimes this is good watching, particularly right now, of course. A scintillating debate is about to take place.
I want to make clear for the record the agreement we have. It is an agreement that seems to have become somewhat clouded over the last few days. The Minister approached the Hon. Member for Cochrane-Superior (Mr. Penner) and I on Monday, in writing, regarding the Bills for today. We collectively struck an agreement some 48 hours ago that Bill C-l 15 would go through the House in all stages today so that it can get off to the Senate and get Royal Assent before the end of this Parliament. By getting our job done today, we are giving effect to the long and hard work that Chief Jules and many others have done, not only in British Columbia but right across Canada.
I know that Chief Jules, in Edmonton yesterday, was carrying on his discussions with George Erasmus, Joe Mathias, George Watts, Conrad Sioe, and many others in relation to this Bill because some concerns were expressed by some in relation to the nature of Bill C-l 15. I think that is quite

June 2, 1988
Indian Act
natural in that it is viewed by some as being a bit of a municipal change to the Indian Act, something that many First Nations avoid. Such a change has an odour that many First Nations do not like to have persist in the atmosphere around them.
Quite frankly, Bill C-115 is not and should not be viewed as some major advance in self-government, nor should it be ruled out as simply some kind of added municipal order. The amendments proposed here have limited but valuable impacts for those bands that wish to use them. The amendments are not some kind of imposition by Parliament on the over 500 bands and the many reserves of Canada.
As my friends both from the government side and from the Official Opposition have said, this is about the right to tax non-Indian interests on conditionally surrendered, or as they will be known, designated lands. Perhaps there is the most urgency coming from British Columbia because of the present tax structures affecting places such as Chief Manny Jules' own home in Kamloops.
B.C. is a little different from most other areas of the country. Other than Governor Douglas' 14 very small treaties on Vancouver Island, and Treaty 8 in northeastern British Columbia and northwestern Alberta, there are no comprehensive settlements in British Columbia and the reserves are very small. We have to reflect on the fact that here we are in the middle of 1988 discussing providing the mechanisms which will allow those very small and impoverished communities to actually tax. This debate should have taken place a century ago. However, we have to compliment the very hard work done by Manny Jules in getting it this far, through second reading this morning and, when the Minister is available this afternoon, through third reading and on to the Senate.
I want to spend a moment on an analysis of Bill C-115 done by a Vancouver lawyer. The analysis was produced in March of this year and makes some interesting points. It says that one must recognize that the amendments do not address all significant areas of Indian concern or the antiquated system of the Indian Act. The amendments do not fundamentally change the land holding system under the Act, nor do they represent any major advance to self-government. The proposed amendments must be thus considered in their context as having the following limited purposes: (a) clarifying the legal characterization of lands which have been surrendered for lease so as to confirm that these lands remain part of the reserve; (b) expanding the powers of Indian Governments to raise revenue on their land from band members as now exists and to include non-Indian businesses on leased land; (c) modifying Section 89 of the Indian Act which protects the property of an Indian from seizure and has the inadvertent consequence of making financing of Indian businesses difficult- that is a point I can certainly confirm from my experience in northwestern British Columbia-and (d) repealing a provision of the Veterans Lands Act.
That is a matter which we are of course going to be dealing with by amendment this afternoon. As I understand it, the original drafters wanted to do it for consequential reasons in relation to other legislation, and in fact an amendment will be moved by the Parliamentary Secretary to delete, I believe, Clause 13 from the legislation.
It should also be noted that these amendments were developed by the Department of Indian Affairs in consultation with and on the initiative of the Kamloops Indian Band. The provincial Government of British Columbia assesses property tax on non-Indian leaseholders of conditionally surrendered lands. The Kamloops Indian Band had faced particular hardship under the existing legislation as it conditionally surrendered some of its lands to create an industrial park and had several non-Indian lessees.
While the province claimed substantial property, school, hospital, and other taxes from those leaseholders, over $7 million in B.C. two years ago, studies show that few services are provided to Indian lands in return. Indian communities such as Kamloops, seeking to develop their lands or lease a portion of these lands, were often required to pay for services to these lands, and the province is acute for all First Nations in B.C. as it is the only province assessing occupiers or lessees of Indian lands.
There is, of course, the Leonard case of 1985 which decided that the personal property tax exemption in Section 87 of the Indian Act applying to income tax, sales tax, tobacco and gasoline taxes, among others, did not apply to transactions occurring on conditionally surrendered lands. This of course created further economic disadvantage for Indian communities that developed lands involving surrenders for the purpose of leasing.
There are some other major applications, but one other which I think should be put on the record concerns Section 87(b) and income tax. An important issue here concerns Indians working for businesses on conditionally surrendered or leased lands. Interpretation Bulletin IT-62 from Revenue Canada considers conditionally surrendered lands to be part of the reserve for the income tax issue. Bulletin IT-62 looks to where the services were performed to determine whether the Indian's income or personal property was situated on a reserve as Section 87 requires. The Supreme Court of Canada case, Nowegijick v. The Queen, decided that an Indian's income or property is situated where the employer is located and where they are paid. This effectively overturned Bulletin IT-62 and it has now been withdrawn. While the Indian remission order continues to recognize the tax exemption for Indians working on reserves, its definition of reserves does not include conditionally surrendered or what is now known as designated lands.
It would therefore appear that an Indian employee, one, working for an employer based on conditionally surrendered lands and working there, or, two, working for an employer based on conditionally surrendered lands and working off reserves, or, three, working for an employer off reserve but
June 2, 1988

doing work on conditionally surrendered lands, will under present law not be able to take advantage of the income tax exemption in Section 87. Under the Bill before us today, however, in all these situations the Indian employee will not be liable to pay income tax because conditionally surrendered lands to be known as designated lands will remain part of the reserve and Section 87 will apply. Those are interesting and important opinions.
The document that was alluded to by the Parliamentary Secretary dealing with proposed amendments to the Indian Act concerning conditionally surrendered land and band taxation powers has, I understand, been made widely available.
I do not agree with all the language, but I think some parts of it are worth putting on the record because its implications, certainly for B.C. bands and others right across the country, are important. I think Hansard may be the best way for that kind of information to be transmitted because it is available in libraries and elsewhere.
The opening page points out that in 1985 the Kamloops Indian Band, led by Chief Manny Jules, made a proposal to amend the Indian Act and a year ago, when this was put out, over 115 band councils had passed resolutions in support of the initiative. The Kamloops Band first became concerned about the question of taxation and conditionally surrendered land in the early 1960s when it established an industrial park on a section of the reserve near the City of Kamloops. The costs of developing the land and providing such basic services as roads, water, and sewage were and continue to be paid by the band. Yet provincial property taxes have always been levied on the park residence. They were therefore put in the position of having to pay service charges for roads, water, sanitation, and the like to the band in addition to property taxes going to the province. This situation inhibited the band in setting lease rates, providing services, and generally in competing with other industrial parks. This is basically a situation which might be described as double taxation.
After many years the band concluded in the early 1980s that it should assert its own powers to levy taxes. In attempting to do so the band encountered basic deficiencies in the Indian Act respecting conditionally surrendered land. Taxation was not the only problem. The band was also concerned about its ability to zone and regulate the land it developed.
It is important to look at the Bill for a moment. While it appears to be quite lengthy, in fact it is not really a terribly complicated piece of legislation in its intent. It amends the definition of "reserve" by adding a definition for "designated lands". It says:
"designated lands" means a tract of land or any interest therein the legal title to which remains vested in Her Majesty and in which the band for whose use and benefit it was set apart as a reserve has, otherwise than absolutely, released or surrendered its rights or interests, whether before or after the coming into force of this definition;
That is really the key part of the Bill. If one then looks at the following pages, one sees that the amendments are consequential for page after page, adding words like
Indian Act
"absolute" or "designation". These kinds of consequential amendments are required in law to make sure that it is clear and consistent throughout. Right through to pages to 4, 4(a), 5, and so on, there are consequential amendments in relation to land and to the definitions of "taxation" and "process".
Those groups that have expressed concern need not worry that it is legislation which brings a massive, broad sweeping change to the Act. It is very limited in its scope and has specific beneficial consequences for groups like the Kamloops Band and many others.
Let me return to the publication which was made broadly available across the country, certainly to municipal and provincial authorities in British Columbia. It went on to state:
In the February 1986 Budget Speech the announcement was made that the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development would bring forward amendments to the Indian Act to enable bands to levy their own local taxes.
Shortly thereafter, the Honourable David Crombie, together with Chief Clarence Jules of the Kamloops Indian Band, issued a press release and wrote to all chiefs and the provincial governments to explain the Budget announcement further, and to launch a process of consultation.
It should be clear for the record that Manny Jules and the Kamloops Band have certainly gone to great lengths in attending meetings of the Union of B.C. Municipalities and in getting information out to other bands. That is evident from the number of positive supporting resolutions. Certainly they have been keeping anyone who is interested, including myself, the Hon.Member for Cochrane-Superior and I am sure the Minister, informed of the importance of getting this through all stages today, perhaps on to the Senate tomorrow, with Royal Assent perhaps by next week.
The document went on to state:
Consultation with Indian leaders was led by Chief Jules, while the Minister and the Department consulted primarily with provincial governments. A number of themes became clear.
First, band taxing powers are an inevitable part of the growth of Indian government. This seemed to be an idea whose time had come.
Second, the status of conditionally surrendered land should be fully clarified such that no other rights are affected or transferred except as necessary to give effect to the wishes of the band in the surrender process. There should be no accidental loss of band jurisdiction or legal rights under the Indian Act.
Third, non Indians on Indian land would be subject to band taxation without having the ability to vote in band elections. Confidence that band taxation would involve appropriate procedures to ensure fairness would be very important.
Fourth, developing good working arrangements with other governments would be important to bands' success in operating taxation and regulatory regimes.
Chief Jules has demonstrated that all those matters have been vigorously and vigilantly pursued.
The document then posed some questions that I believe some people in the House and others across the country might ask:
What is surrendered land?
Under the Indian Act, Indian reserves are held by the Crown for the 'use and benefit' of Indian bands. Bands must 'surrender' their rights in reserve

June 2, 1988
Indian Act
land to the federal government before the government can give possession of it, by sale or lease, to non-Indians.
Again, certainly in British Columbia, it comes back to the real, legitimate, and constitutionally required and prescribed need to settle the comprehensive claims in British Columbia. Obviously this would be pursuant to the full box of Section 35 of the Constitution which recognizes and affirms aboriginal rights and treaty rights in Canada.
There is beginning to be some clarification in British Columbia, through the Gitksan Wet'suwet'en case before the Supreme Court, and, without question, from the famed Nisga-Calder case that went before the Supreme Court of Canada some 16 years ago. The Justices of the Supreme Court unanimously recognized the continuing existence of aboriginal title.
It is only a matter of getting some kind of positive maturity from the Government of British Columbia to move forward and seriously settle the outstanding comprehensive claims in British Columbia. As anyone can see, the land rights provided under the Indian Act, as reserves in British Columbia, provides few benefits indeed.
Let me return to the document. It continued:
From the first version of the Indian Act in 1868 to today, except under certain restricted circumstances, no part of an Indian reserve can be leased or sold on behalf of a band unless it has first been 'surrendered'.
The next question posed in the document was: What is "conditionally" surrendered land? It stated:
In apparent recognition of this fact, the 1951 version of the Indian Act included a new reference to the old concept of surrender. Section 38(2) says, 'A surrender may be absolute or qualified, conditional or unconditional'. Nothing more was said as to how a 'conditional' surrender should be applied throughout the rest of the Act. The vitally important difference between conditional and unconditional surrender was recognized but not defined.
Subsequently, the Courts decided that land conditionally surrendered for lease retains a fundamental Indian interest. It remains 'land reserved for the Indians' under Section 91(24) of the Constitution Act, 1867. This means that Parliament has the exclusive power to pass laws affecting such land. Provincial laws or by-laws of municipalities which are land-related cannot be enforced on conditionally surrendered land, even against non-Indian leaseholders. Property taxation is an exception to this general rule for certain reasons-
I will now touch on those reasons.
The next question asked in the document was: What is the problem with conditionally surrendered land? As we deal with this debate, we realize that the rights provided to aboriginal people all across the country, certainly in British Columbia, is extremely limited. That has been the historical problem in raising funds to develop a business on reserve, to get a mortgage to build a home, or to use any of the kind of acquired rights that almost any other Canadian would find when one has title fee simple, whether to a small lot in the city or to a piece of land anywhere else in the country.
Even a lease or almost any other kind of title will provide a much greater potential financial instrument than the reserve situation as it has been allowed to rest since 1867.
The primary benefit of conditional surrender is clear: It enables land to be leased without losing its status as Indian land. This should mean that Indian bands can develop their land through lease arrangements without having to give up their underlying 'ownership' of it, their local government powers over it, or their special rights on it; all of which are fundamental to reserve land status. The only rights that are affected should be those that are necessary to the purpose and conditions of the surrender and the terms of the lease.
I encourage those who are interested in looking at the sections dealing with tax and tax power to obtain this document. I am sure the Parliamentary Secretary would be pleased to provide it to anyone who wants to write to him.
Section C asked why bands needed jurisdiction over their land and indicated:
A regulatory vacuum.
One of the most important court decisions concerning jurisdiction on Indian land was a 1970 decision of the British Columbia Court of Appeal ('Surrey v. Peace Arch Enterprises Ltd.) The Court decided that reserve lands conditionally surrendered to the Crown and then leased to developers for an amusement park were not subject to municipal zoning and other by-laws and regulations specifying building, water service, sewage disposal and other requirements with respect to the land and the way it could and could not be used. The lands remained 'lands reserved for the Indians' under exclusive federal jurisdiction.
The Committee asked, 'who can control the planning and development of Indian lands in British Columbia?' Considering the Peace Arch case and the deficiencies of the Indian Act, the answer appears effectively to be-no one except Parliament itself.
We must ask ourselves how this is possible not only in terms of the Kamloops Band which has helped to bring this proposed amendment to the Indian Act forward. Again, this leads to the argument my friend from Cochrane-Superior did not want to enter today, that the real debate which should be taking place on the floor of the House is in terms of self-government and devolution.
It is frankly impossible, with over 590 bands in Canada and with the kinds of decisions that have been taken by the Supreme Court of Canada, the Superior Courts, the provinces, and the territories, right across this land, on issues such as the one before us today. We are tinkering today-and it is important tinkering in that it is going to provide some small tools-but there is a more fundamental and much more highly principled debate that will soon take place in providing all the broader government rights to aboriginal people. Therefore, I am pleased to have participated this morning and this afternoon in second reading. Shortly after lunch, I understand, I look forward to completing Committee of the Whole and third reading stages and sending the Bill on to the Senate so that Chief Jules knows when to turn that TV back on in Edmonton and see the success.

speechtext: that Bill C-122, an Act to amend the Indian Act (by-laws and membership rules), be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.

speakeroldname: Mr. Stan Schellenberger (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, you are moving us right along today in your usual good way. I am pleased to speak to Bill C-122, which amends the Indian Act in order to help address the issue of enforceability and validity of enacted band by-laws and membership rules. As Hon. Members know, this Government is firmly committed to the concept of Indian self-governmemt. We have taken several important steps in this respect since coming to office, including passing self-government enabling legislation for the Sechelt Band in British Columbia. The Cree and Naskapi Bands in Quebec are also operating under a system of self-government, and discussions are ongoing with other bands on the development of new and unique systems of selfgovernment.
Canada's Indian people are also assuming more control over their day-to-day lives through the process called "devolution", which is the transfer to Indian communities of authority for local programs and services. In many cases, the bands are using this process as a stepping stone to broader self-government arrangements.
Despite our commitment to increased Indian autonomy and the clear self-government aspirations of native people, the fact remains that most bands will continue to be governed by provisions of the Indian Act into the foreseeable future. We must, therefore, ensure that the processes by which the bands develop and implement by-laws and membership rules will be sensitive to native concerns and at the same time will not be adversely affected by the enforceability of by-laws and membership rules. Bill C-122 achieves that by simplifying those processes which safeguard the right of band members to be informed of membership rules and local by-laws.
Indian Act
I would like to take a few moments to provide Members with some brief background of this legislation. Under the Statutory Instruments Act, by-laws and membership rules of Indian bands must be examined, registered, and published in the same manner as other federal regulations. This means that they must be published in The Canada Gazette. While the federal Government has an important role to play in ensuring that the band enactments meet the criteria set out in the Statutory Instruments Act, we do not wish to restrict unduly the ability of elected band councils to establish membership rules and pass by-laws necessary for the good government of their communities.
On March 20, 1987, the Standing Joint Committee on Regulations and other Statutory Instruments presented its fifth report to the House of Commons and Senate. In this report, the committee outlined the difficulties encountered in discharging its mandate in relationship to by-laws made by Indian band councils. The Standing Committee also detailed its concerns over how by-laws are dealt with by federal Government and Indian bands.
The Standing Joint Committee concerns are well founded. I would like to commend its members for bringing these problems to light. The committee's recommendations were given careful consideration in the development of the Bill before us today. I am confident that this Bill will satisfy the committee's concerns. Under the existing provisions of the Indian Act, there is a very real possibility that by-laws and membership rules, passed prior to June 28, 1987, did not conform to the applicable requirements of the Statutory Instruments Act and could be declared unenforceable. It is for this reason that we require quick passage of Bill C-122.
This legislation strikes a balance between two important considerations. First, it ensures that band councils will have the authority to develop and enforce fair and valid by-laws and membership rules, but, just as important, it ensures that these by-laws and membership rules will be widely available for scrutiny by band members who are affected by them.
Not every band member receives The Canada Gazette. I do not know how many of us actually read it every day, and I am sure many of them do not. That is why this is so important. Requiring bands to conform to the stringent provisions of the Statutory Instruments Act complicates the process of band decision making, and it is seen by many bands as a unwarranted interference in their affairs.
Bill C-122, therefore, amends the Indian Act to exempt band membership rules established under Section 10 and bylaws made under Sections 81, 83, and 85, subsection 1, from examination, registration, and publication in The Canada Gazette. This will not provide by-laws and membership rules from public scrutiny. As I stated earlier, Bill C-122 contains important provisions regarding notification to band members. Band councils will be required to publish a notice of the band's membership rules in a local newspaper or post the notice in a conspicuous place on the reserve. The notice must include a

June 2, 1988
Indian Act
summary of rules and indicate a location on the reserve where the full context of the rules can be found for review or purchase by anyone interested.
The legislation also requires band councils to publish a notice of all by-laws in a local newspaper. Bill C-122 also repeals and replaces Section 86 of the Indian Act. This amendment will enable a superintendent or secretary of the band to issue true certified copies of by-laws and membership rules, will allow certified true copies to be received in evidence without proof of signature, and will ensure that by-laws and membership rules are not invalid by reason of any defect in form.
Finally, Bill C-122 amends the Indian Act to ensure that existing by-laws and membership rules are not declared invalid simply because they were not processed in accordance with provisions of the Statutory Instruments Act. These amendments will not be considered retroactive for cases now before the courts.
Bill C-122 calls for simple but important technical amendments to the Indian Act. The legislation reflects this Government's themes of progress, fairness, and keeping its commitments to native people.
This House has previously demonstrated its support for Indian concerns and aspirations. I am happy to see that we are moving this Bill into committee today so that we can have a further detailed study of it to ensure that it is acceptable and, hopefully, to put it in place for Indian people in the near future.

Mr. Speaker, it will be my intention in participating in this debate to indicate to the House that this Bill, Bill C-122, is far more than merely some technical amendments to the Indian Act, and that there are some far-reaching and undesirable consequences of it which will make it unacceptable to myself and to this Party.
Let me begin with some background and lead up to my objections to Bill C-122. The raison d'etre for this legislation, says the Government in its communique giving the background to this Bill, is to "advance and promote Indian self-government". The Government argues that it does not want to restrict unduly the freedom of democratically elected band councils to pass local by-laws that are necessary for the good government of their communities. So says the propaganda. The Government of Canada does not want to interfere unduly in how such by-laws are enacted or implemented. The objective of the legislation is to exempt the band councils, in the case, for example, of their membership rules and other bylaws, from the application of the Statutory Instruments Act.
On the surface that may appear to be technical. In due course I want to show that it is much more than technical. At the same time this Bill provides what are considered to be
guarantees that proper notice will be given to all persons likely to be affected by such band council enactments.
A couple of points must be made in dealing with the principle of this Bill. The first point is that it is pretentious, pompous, even misleading of the Government to make the fatuous claim that Bill C-122 in some way advances or promotes Indian self-government. I reject that as a claim. I reject that as being in any way a principle of this Bill.
The Special Committee on Indian Self-Government made it very clear that amending the Indian Act can never be a route to self-government. I quote from that report which states: "The antiquated policy basis and structure of the Indian Act make it completely unacceptable as a blueprint for the future".
Piecemeal changes to the Indian Act can never achieve the self-determination which Indian people are seeking. So the question must be asked: Why, today, is the Government tinkering again with the Indian Act in terms of what is proposed in Bill C-122? The real reason is the Government's past failure to comply with the Statutory Instruments Act with regard to the registration and the publication of band membership codes brought into being by virtue of Section 10 of the Indian Act.
The Government sought to end run or get away from the obligation under the Statutory Instruments Act by issuing an Order in Council on June 25, 1987, purporting to exempt band membership codes from the provisions of the Statutory Instruments Act. When the Native Council of Canada discovered this, it regarded the action in this Order in Council to be potentially invalid and certainly undesirable.
The interesting thing is that on closer examination the Order in Council did much, much more than simply exempt the band membership codes from registration and publication under the Statutory Instruments Act. It in fact exempted all by-laws passed by band councils from the registration, the examination, and the publication requirements of the Statutory Instruments Act.
Thus at first the Government tried to get away with it. Then it tried to circumvent the law by Order in Council. In both cases it failed to live up to the legal requirements of good government. Now, to clean up this mess it has decided to legislate, and to do so in Bill C-122.
The Minister advised bands and the aboriginal people's organizations that this was going to be done. They were asked to respond by a certain date, that is, February 28 of this year. They were asked to respond on February 28 in a letter that was dated February 15. Those of us who are aware of the postal service in Canada will know that those letters did not reach a large number of bands until the end of February, or in some cases early in March.
I ask you, Mr. Speaker, is it any wonder that in Canada the word "consultation" when it comes to dealing with Indian people has become a dirty word? I am sure the Minister would argue that consultation had taken place. The Native Council
June 2, 1988

of Canada, which has a very special interest in band membership by-laws, because so many of its members are pursuing reinstatement under Bill C-31, were not even notified at all of the Government's intentions.
I want the House to know that Bill C-122 has been mishandled. If that were all there was to it, we could be forgiving because Governments by definition mishandle almost everything they touch. It is not the mishandling that I am so distressed about, although it is bothersome, but that this legislation is wrong-headed. It cannot be supported.
Bill C-122 will place new responsibilities on bands to publicize new by-laws. This Bill will require bands to post notices about new by-laws in a conspicuous place, to have the by-laws available to the public for examination, and to place notices in local newspapers.
Some lawyers quite rightly argued and pointed out that if the band is not extremely careful and most scrupulous in this obligation their new by-laws may in fact be null and void. They may have great difficulty enforcing them.
There is a more serious matter than that. That more serious matter is the Bill's provision to exempt all band by-laws from registration as statutory instruments. Bands do not want the legal status of their by-laws to be diminished in that manner, and that is the key point I want to make in explaining why Bill C-122 is unacceptable to us. It is not as innocuous as it seems at first blush. It does something quite detrimental to the nature of all band by-laws. The chiefs at the Assembly of First Nations meeting in Edmonton yesterday passed a resolution totally rejecting the Bill. They did so because the Bill exempts all band by-laws from registration as statutory instruments, as well as exempting them from examination and publication under the Statutory Instruments Act.
The exemption from registration appears to imply that all band by-laws from now on will not be considered as statutory instruments. That is serious. Indian bands have won some very important fishing cases in courts in this country because the courts have said that their fishing by-laws are statutory instruments which therefore supersede provincial legislation and regulations. If their by-laws lose their status as statutory instruments, as Bill C-122 proposes, then the legal status of bands and the by-laws that they pass will be diminished.
In the past, by-laws have been exempted from examination and publication. This Bill goes further by exempting future bylaws from registration. The Native Council of Canada opposes the Bill for its exemption of membership by-laws from examination or publication. The Assembly of First Nations opposes the Bill for taking away the statutory instruments of their by-laws.
Finally, when this Bill goes to committee, as it certainly will because the Government dominates the House with its majority, it will be seen whether or not the First Nations
Indian Act
object to the process of passing by-laws contained in this Bill. The process is very much on the municipal model. Most First Nations negatively view the concept that they are no more than federally recognized municipalities. The report of the special committee made it clear that Indian government, aboriginal government in this country, is a distinct order. It is not federal, it is not provincial, and it is not municipal. It is a distinct order of Government and must be so recognized.
The Assembly of First Nations in Edmonton have rejected Bill C-122. They are concerned that the Bill would mean that by-laws would no longer be considered as statutory instruments. I have explained to you, and to my colleagues in the House, the legal importance of that when there are court cases pending with respect to fishing rights and other aboriginal rights.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, when you put the question to the House, I will ask that Bill C-122 be carried on division. I want it to be clearly indicated that I and members of my Party, the Official Opposition, do not support Bill C-122.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Does the Hon. Member for Skeena wish to speak longer than five minutes?

I will attempt to keep my remarks to one o'clock, Mr. Speaker.
Like the Hon. Member for Cochrane-Superior (Mr. Penner), I have extremely serious concerns about Bill C-122. For those people who are watching or listening to this debate, it should be made clear that, in bringing five Bills before the House today, it is a bit of a grab-bag routine. One gets the good, the bad, and the ugly. Bill C-122 is what I would describe as ugly legislation.
Earlier this morning we dealt with Bill C-102 which clearly was required. It is supported by the Inuvialuit and I am sure by all First Nations. Bill C-115 is broadly supported by First Nations across the country. This afternoon we will be debating Indian lands in Ontario. There are two sides to the debate, but again it has broad support and enormous implications for more than 200,000 acres of land that have been in a grey area of title since 1867, and similarly since 1924.
Bill C-122 is ugly in that it is Trojan horse legislation. If one was solely to read the media pulp coming out of the Minister's office, one would think that what the Government is doing is saving the complicated procedure of having to mail in by-laws, published in The Canada Gazette, and scrutinized by the Joint Standing Committee on Statutory Instruments of the two Houses. By publishing them in local newspapers and posting them in an open and visible place in local communities, that is somehow cutting back on a bureaucratic problem.
My friend, the Hon. Member for Cochrane-Superior (Mr. Penner) who just spoke, pointed out that there are extremely fundamental legal issues associated with this proposal. I am sure the witnesses we hear before the committee will make it clear that this Bill should be amended down to zero.

June 2, 1988
Although a few months ago the Standing Joint Committee on Regulations and Statutory Instruments filed a lengthy report that I would encourage Members to read, the facts of the matter are that the Opposition put forward a resolution by the Assembly of First Nations in Edmonton yesterday based on good foundation. My friend referred to by-laws. I know only too well of some of those by-laws that the former Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development passed that became tied up in the courts in relation to the Gitksan-Wet'suwet'en by-laws on the Skeena.
There are many fishing and other cases that have succeeded based on the existing structure, albeit rife with problems as identified by members of the standing joint committee, but not simply to tear up the existing section of the Indian Act and amend it in this manner. One need only look at the multitude of press releases that come from the Minister, and information circulars and so on which make it seem that this is a nice way of tidying things up. That could hardly be further from the case. Even some publications make it sound as though it is only getting rid of some red tape and some localized problems in relation to alcohol by-laws, and so on. Nothing could be further from the case, even as is admitted by the members of the standing joint committee.
I wish to read a couple of brief quotations from their fifth report:
The Statutory Instruments Act subjects all by-laws made under the Indian Act to review and scrutiny by your Joint Committee in accordance with the statutory reference set out in section 126 of the Act. From 1982 to 1985, the Joint Committee examined by-laws made pursuant to sections 81 and 83 of the Indian Act on a regular basis. The Joint Committee's general findings as to the degree of conformity of many by-laws to its scrutiny criteria are recorded in the correspondence reproduced in Appendix 'B' to this report. Your Committee concluded that its scrutiny of by-laws made under the Indian Act serves a limited practical purpose at best, and that it would not henceforth review these on an individual basis.
Here we have a committee and statutory instruments based on law passed by this Parliament in 1972 that are not being scrutinized by the joint standing committee. They do not want to have to keep looking at it. They point out problems with bylaws made under Section 81 of the Act which can only come into force 40 days after a copy of the by-law is forwarded to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. McKnight), unless the Minister declares it to be in force before the expiration of that period. They certainly outline problems found with the procedures.
I could not say it more strongly, Mr. Speaker, that all Members of the House should oppose Bill C-122. I certainly oppose it in principle, and in terms of how it is laid out, in terms of how it is portrayed to the nation and to the first nations. I oppose it, my Party opposes it, and I am sure that when we hear witnesses before the legislative committee we will find that it will necessarily be amended to zero and not see the light of day.

subsubtopic: SUPPORT URGED FOR RESEARCH INTO LOU GEHRIG'S DISEASE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the week of June 1 to 7 has been declared Flower Week by the municipalities across the country. Flower Week is the one time each year we are asked to remember those of our fellow Canadians who have been diagnosed as having a progressive degenerative disease called ALS. Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, often called Lou Gehrig's disease, causes paralysis, loss of speech, and difficulties with breathing and swallowing. Life expectancy is only three years after diagnosis. What a terrifying thought that is.
ALS strikes as many people as multiple sclerosis yet we hear so little about this debilitating disease. During this Flower Week volunteers will be fanning out across Canada asking for our support and offering the traditional corn flower which is the national symbol of the ALS Society. This money is truly needed by this worthy society as they are attempting to raise funds for research into the cause of this killer disease and possibly to find a cure.
I urge all Members and all Canadians to support this deserving cause. Wear a corn flower and, as Lou Gehrig would say, help strike out ALS.

Mr. Speaker, as you know, this is National Environment Week. It is appropriate
June 2, 1988

and timely, therefore, to review the preliminary results of a study released by the Ontario Ministry of the Environment.
The backdrop to this study is the declaration of intent signed by Canada and the United States which commits both countries to cut in half by 1996 the levels of persistent toxic chemicals in the Niagara River. This is a positive step forward. However, a new study indicates that, despite clean-up efforts, highly toxic chemicals from the United States continue to seep into the Niagara River.
Environment Week reminds us that we must continue to be vigilant and remind our American friends that they have a responsibility for completely cleaning up the mess they have made.

Mr. Speaker, two years ago I visited a small community on the outskirts of Lima, Peru. Fifteen years earlier families had moved onto the area as squatters and built shelters out of woven mats. Gradually they replaced the mats with brick, but they had no water and had to purchase it by the barrel, which was both expensive and unsanitary.
Later the community dug an 80 metre well and put in basic plumbing, and Canada provided a pump. When Ambassador Keith Bezanson pressed the button and a four-inch stream of water began to flow, rusty at first but later clearer, everyone cheered and danced. This wasn't just a pump, this was water.
One hundred years ago Ludwig Feuerbach talked about the material basis of life and said: "Therefore let bread be sacred for us, let wine be sacred and also let water be sacred".
During this Environment Week when Ottawa hosts the World Congress on Water Resources we need to remember the importance of water for our cities, our farms, our fisheries, and our forests, for all the peoples of the world. For us let water be sacred.

Mr. Speaker, Buona Festa to all our Italian friends! Forty-two years ago, Italy became a republic, and will celebrate this anniversary next Sunday.
We have a commonality of ancestors and cultures that goes back to the conquest of Gaul by Julius Caesar, which is probably why we seem to have much in common with the millions of Canadians who are of Italian origin.
On behalf of my constituents in the riding of La Prairie who are of Italian origin and on behalf of all Canadians, we wish to offer the President of the Republic of Italy, Mr. Francesco Cossiga, and the Italian government and the people of that wonderful country, our best wishes on that important day.

subtopic: MONITORING OF GREAT LAKES BY GREENPEACE SHIP
MONITORING OF GREAT LAKES BY GREENPEACE SHIP
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as you know, Greenpeace is a great Canadian institution. It has served the environment well at home and abroad since its inception in Vancouver in 1971. Right now its ship, the Beluga, is touring the Great Lakes. Joyce McLean, the Greenpeace Great Lakes campaign co-ordinator, explains why. She says:
Our purpose-is to support local anti-pollution efforts... We believe the
public is frustrated with the lack of restrictive legislation concerning ongoing
industrial pollution.
Clearly there is a big gap between the declaration of intentions in the Great Lakes Water Quality Agreement and the daily reality.
The Beluga has identified many instances where serious pollution is caused by industrial and domestic waste and by human activities. Greenpeace deserves the support of Canadians and the full co-operation of governments at all levels. In identifying the causes of pollution Greenpeace plays an invaluable role in the cleaning up of the Great Lakes.

speakeroldname: Mr. Blaine A. Thacker (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, recently several articles have appeared in West Coast newspapers implying that Bill C-52 will severely damage the cruise ship industry on the West Coast.
Bill C-52, which has been passed by this House and is currently before the other place, reserves the carriage of goods and passengers from one port in Canada to another port or the same port in Canada to Canadian ships. When no suitable

June 2, 1988
Canadian ships are available, a flag waiver will be given so foreign ships may offer the service.
In recognition of the economic benefit to Canada of the cruise ship industry, particularly on the West Coast, cruise ships having overnight passenger accommodation of 250 or more have been specifically exempted from the provisions of Bill C-52. This means that they do not have to apply for a flag waiver but may carry on their business freely.
Press reports state that Bill C-52 will impose new duties and taxes on these ships. This is not so. All duties and taxes are imposed by tax legislation, and all decisions about what moneys are to be collected on these ships are made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson). Bill C-52 does not amend tax legislation.
The B.C. Members of Parliament have not let down the people of British Columbia.

Mr. Speaker, the City of Hamilton recently endorsed a resolution condemning the Government of Canada for its supermailbox program. The resolution calls for an immediate halt to the installation of supermailboxes and for the restoration of home delivery to all affected residences.
I rise today in support of this resolution. Supermailboxes are often mud splattered, prone to vandalism, and frequently surrounded by discarded junk mail. They are inaccessible to the disabled and can be quite some distance from people's homes, making it difficult for seniors and others to collect their mail.
The supermailbox program is an affront to the citizens of Canada and a violation of Canada Post's mandate to "provide a standard of service that will meet the needs of the people of Canada". The program effectively makes second-class citizens of urban dwellers by forcing them to accept this type of inferior postal service.
I join with the citizens of Hamilton in condemning the Government for its supermailbox program. Hamiltonians call for the immediate abandonment of Canada Post's corporate plan and the reinstatement of home delivery to all urban residences.

Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the constituents of Kitchener I would like to congratulate the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mrs. McDougall) for her recent amendments to the immigration regulations.
Effective July 8, the current policy of permitting family-class sponsorship of only those unmarried children under 21 years of age will now be expanded to allow the sponsorship of never married children of any age. Also, never married children of any age will be able to accompany immigrants in any category as dependants. Other changes will further assist married sons and daughters and sisters and brothers applying under the assisted relative category.
This new policy is consistent with Canada's approach to family reunification and genuine refugees, and its effectiveness will be greatly enhanced with the passage of Bills C-55 and C-84. These two Bills are designed to prohibit the abuse of our immigration system by phoney refugees and queue jumpers. As a result, Canada's immigration policy will be both compassionate and fair to those who respect the process, and tough and decisive on those who do not.

CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-PRINTING INDUSTRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, every day we hear of more and more Canadians who will lose their jobs and be casualties of the Prime Minister's (Mr. Mulroney) trade deal.
Yesterday I received a letter from the Canadian Printing Industries Association concerning the effects of this deal. The Canadian Printing Industries Association has recently commissioned and received a report prepared by the prestigious Montreal consulting firm of Samson, Belair which says:
The industry will lose 3,000 jobs as a result of the free trade agreement unless the Government puts in place adjustment programs dealing with some of the structural weaknesses identified.
The sad reality is that under this lousy trade deal adjustment programs are not even provided for and may even be countervailable as an unfair subsidy.
More and more we find out that this deal is bad for Canada and for Canadian workers.
June 2, 1988

Mr. Speaker, the United Nations World Commission on Environment and Development has concluded that the world, in order to safeguard the environment which is the ultimate base of all economic activity, must work to attain sustainable development. All Canadians can work toward this goal during this week, National Environment Week, and throughout the year in a small but significant way by recycling and reusing as much as possible the 500 kilograms of garbage each of us disposes of each year at a total national cost of $1.5 billion.
O)
The Brundtland Commission has warned that our environment cannot sustain single-use throw-away products. Hundreds of items in our everyday garbage are indeed recyclables, including paper, glass and other items. Environment Week is a time to bundle it up. It is up to all of us to keep Canada clean, to keep Canada prosperous.
 * *

Mr. Speaker, reading the daily newspapers can really put one off celebrating Environment Week. For example, there is one story today about the 27 nuclear facilities around the Great Lakes, the lakes from which roughly 40 million Canadians and Americans get their drinking water.
An accident at any one of these nuclear reactors could be disastrous for that number of people. However, what does the nuclear industry say? It says that the storage is safe and that a little bit of tritium will not do us any harm.
There is also a story today about the fact that more toxic chemicals are showing up in the Niagara River than previously, despite the existence of an agreement on clean-up and the beginning of clean-up in some areas. Clearly the clean-up programs in place are inadequate right now and far more of these sites need to be cleaned up. Canadians would prefer to celebrate Environment Week with real clean-up and action and not a public relations program.

Member for Kootenay West (Mr. Brisco), the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark), and the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. McKnight) because, together with other Hon. CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-HEALTH SERVICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a few moments ago the Minister of Health in Ontario announced the introduction of the Independent Health Facilities Act. This Act will give the Ontario Government the right to discriminate in favour of not-for-profit and Canadian operators in the provision of health services in the Province of Ontario.
We have heard time and again from the federal Government that the free trade deal has absolutely nothing to do with health care services, but according to the federal Government's legislation we cannot discriminate in favour of non-profit and Canadian operators in the provision of health care services because the deal says we have to give national treatment to health care services. You must have non-discrimination. This potentially violates clauses on services and investment.
I challenge the federal Government to lay it on the line. It should drop this section of the free trade agreement dealing with the ability of Ontario to promote non-profit health services. We want non-profit health services in Ontario. We want to support the Ontario Government's Bill. Yet the trade deal may prevent that.
Wake up, Canadians, the health of your children is on the line in this deal. The federal Government should drop health care services from the free trade agreement.

Mr. Speaker, for years Saskatchewan boasted of having the lowest or second lowest rate of unemployment in the country. Succeeding Governments have been proud of this record of achievement. My province has now added a second place rating in another
level of economic statistics. However, this time we do not take any pride in it.
The facts are that one in five people in Saskatchewan now live in poverty. Newfoundland is the only other province with a worse record. There, 22.8 per cent of the population lives in poverty. In Saskatchewan, 16.4 per cent of all families live in poverty. What is more disturbing is the poverty level of children. In our province more than 25 per cent, or 64,600 children, live in poverty compared to 26 per cent in Newfoundland. The national average is 17.6 per cent.
What a terrible legacy considering that Conservative Governments at both federal and provincial levels have always said that the family is their number one priority. That is great rhetoric but it is no consolation to the families or children of Saskatchewan.

speechtext: The Hon. Member for Oshawa.

subsubtopic: INCREASE IN BANK OF CANADA INTEREST RATE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Minister of Finance my question is directed to the Minister of State for Finance.

A few minutes ago, the Bank of Canada announced an increase in the bank rate of one-third of a point. This kind of decision will have a negative impact on our exports because of its effect on the Canadian dollar. In the past, the Governments of Quebec and Ontario have taken a stand against this policy, and recently, the same kind of stand was taken in Western Canada. My question is this: why does the Government of Canada support the Bank of Canada's policy, which has a negative impact on Canada's economy?

subsubtopic: INCREASE IN BANK OF CANADA INTEREST RATE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure my hon. friend remembers back to November, 1981, when this country had interest rates over 20 per cent. That is why we are supporting the Bank of Canada's policy. We do not want interest rates to get out of hand here in Canada.
Let me tell the Hon. Member what has happened. Business intentions for investment are at an all-time high. Demand is very, very strong. Profits are good. Housing starts are at near record levels. We have a very, very strong economy with strong demand. We do not want this to get out of hand. So what has happened is we have all this heat running through the pipe of the Canadian economy. We do not want an explosion of huge, huge inflation and interest rates at the other end. That is why we support the Governor of the Bank of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, spoken just like the Chairman of the Royal Bank or any of the other chartered banks. I can tell the Minister that the Premiers of all the western provinces, the Premier of Ontario, the Premier of

Quebec, as well as the Manufacturers' Association, and the Association of Agricultural Producers-almost every group in every section of the country-are against the Government of Canada's policy in support of the Bank of Canada.
Since the Minister of Finance at the time of his Budget announced-

speechtext: What about free trade, Ed?
