speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister has been courteous, if not his colleagues, in answering the question. I would like him to deal with a second question.
The Minister of Finance in the budget documents stated that a 1 per cent drop in interest rates reduces the charges on the Canadian debt paid by the Canadian taxpayers by $1.4 billion annually. If these interest rates continue to go up and there is a 1 per cent increase will this amount to a roughly $ 1.4 billion increase to the Canadian taxpayers in terms of paying charges on the Canadian debt?

subtopic: EFFECT OF INTEREST RATES ON TAXPAYERS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member's question fell into two parts. First, he asked me about the regional impact of interest rates. I do not know whether the Hon. Member is suggesting that we have a monetary policy for Quebec, and another monetary policy for a different region of Canada.

subtopic: EFFECT OF INTEREST RATES ON TAXPAYERS
speechtext: They're all in agreement.

subtopic: EFFECT OF INTEREST RATES ON TAXPAYERS
speechtext:
What is very interesting-and I hope that the Hon. Member will listen carefully to me since I listened to his question-is that if we had in this country a monetary policy based upon southern Ontario, Oshawa, London, Toronto, and places like that, interest rates would be much higher. Instead we base monetary policy in this country on national statistics, national demand, and national supply. The interest rate policy as a result of that is more moderate than it would be if it were based on southern Ontario alone.
The second point which is important to realize is that commodity prices in this country-pulp and paper, raw fish, zinc, copper, aluminum-all of which affect the regions of Canada outside southern Ontario, are also high. Thus the whole country wants us to have a moderate interest rate policy, and that is what we have.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister has just acknowledged that there is a significant difference, in his opinion, between the different regions in terms of the interest rate policy that would be appropriate.
Since I have a communique from the western Premiers who have joined Premier Bourassa of Quebec-
Oral Questions

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: Who all supported free trade.

-and Premier Peterson of Ontario in unanimously calling for a lower interest rate policy, and considering that we in the Opposition have done the same, as have manufacturers and farmers, why does the Government not do what the people of Canada want instead of what the Bank of Canada wants?
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member is very careful when he quotes those Premiers. When they support free trade he is not in favour of what they say.
When these Premiers ask questions about interest rates, we listen. We make sure that we have a monetary policy based for all of Canada, not just Oshawa, Toronto, or London, Ontario.

Mr. Speaker, my question concerns the proposed resolution before the British Cabinet on labelling of fur products from Canada. An all-Party House of Commons committee reported to the House in December of 1986 stating: "Steel-toothed leghold traps are no longer used by Canadian trappers and have not been manufactured in North America for well over a decade."
The Government is having no results whatsoever in dealing with the British Cabinet. The Secretary of State for External Affairs said in the House last night:
-the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs ..., raised the matter at recent talks in London ... I also raised the subject in the course of bilateral discussions with Sir Geoffrey Howe... The Prime Minister-discussed the matter during his conversations with Mrs. Thatcher, who said she wanted to obtain more information on the subject.
What more information does Margaret Thatcher need? Or is this just another example of this Government's problem in communication?
Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Hon. Bill McKnight (Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):

Mr. Speaker, I would like to draw to the attention of the House once again the participation in the debate last night of all three political Parties.

June 2, 1988

I would like to inform the Hon. Member that since the notification that is necessary to move this legislation in the British Parliament has not taken place, there is now a delay, a delay that we feel is important to Canada so that we can make our case once more. I believe that everyone would recognize that, rather than proceed as it could have with this piece of legislation, a delay is a good sign for Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I am sure the Minister will agree that if the British Cabinet passes this resolution then the next logical step would be to outlaw leather shoes, leather briefcases, or leather clothing, and certainly the consumption of meat products. Can you imagine, Mr. Speaker, the British doing without roast beef and Yorkshire pudding, or steak and kidney pie?
If the British Government is intent on destroying the Canadian fur industry with false labels and information, is the Government prepared to tell the British that we will cut back on our business with them, and that they can take their nuclear submarine and sink it?

speakeroldname: Hon. Bill McKnight (Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Minister of the Western Diversification Office; Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development

Mr. Speaker, I know the Hon. Member is concerned about leather-that includes leather lungs.
What we have to understand is that it is not only the Canadian Government that recognizes that Great Britain does business with Canada. The trappers and aboriginal people in Canada recognize that certain companies such as Marks & Spencer, Boots Drugs, and Cadbury's, do business in Canada. They are prepared to take action and ask other Canadians to join them which I, as an individual am prepared to do, as I am sure is the Hon. Member.
What one has to understand is that we cannot settle this in Canada. It has to be settled in the Parliament of Great Britain. That is why the Prime Minister has taken an interest in it, as has the Secretary of State for External Affairs, and why all Parties in the House last evening took part in a very historic debate.

subsubtopic: ELIMINATION OF TWO-PRICE WHEAT SYSTEM-EFFECT ON CONSUMERS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Agriculture. Over the past couple of years Canadian consumers have paid something near the cost of production for products which contain wheat, such as pasta, bread, and other products. With the Government's announcement yesterday of the elimination of the two-price wheat program beginning April 2, consumers should see a measurable drop in the price they pay for wheat based products such as bread. What measures will the Government take to ensure that these savings are in fact passed on to the consumer?

subsubtopic: ELIMINATION OF TWO-PRICE WHEAT SYSTEM-EFFECT ON CONSUMERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 certainly appreciate the question of the Hon. Member and, indeed, the thrust and thinking behind it.
I think it was very obvious that my colleague, in making the announcement on the two-price wheat issue yesterday, signalled the high expectations that, when phasing out of the two-price wheat system comes into effect after the next crop year, one would fully expect that the savings would be passed on and definitely be reflected in consumer prices.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR ASSURANCE CONSUMERS WILL RECEIVE FULL BENEFIT
REQUEST FOR ASSURANCE CONSUMERS WILL RECEIVE FULL BENEFIT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is directed to the Minister responsible for Consumer Affairs. Canadian consumers know that generally prices go up and hardly ever come down. With the drop in the domestic price of wheat, we can calculate almost exactly what should be the reduction passed on to the consumer.
June 2, 1988

Would the Minister assure consumers that they will definitely receive the full benefit of the elimination of the two-price wheat program?

Member that my Department will be watching bread prices very closely, and using whatever authorities are available to ensure that the consumer receives the full benefit of any reduction in the cost of wheat that goes into making bread.

subtopic: ELIMINATION OF TWO-PRICE WHEAT SYSTEM-ONE-YEAR ADJUSTMENT PROGRAM
ELIMINATION OF TWO-PRICE WHEAT SYSTEM-ONE-YEAR ADJUSTMENT PROGRAM
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Agriculture. The Canadian wheat growers have been receiving some $280 million per year benefit from the two-price wheat system. Now that this is being cut out due to the Prime Minister's trade agreement with the United States, why will the Government only provide an adjustment program for one year when the United States is increasing its support to its producers under the Export Enhancement Program and other programs, and we are cutting out this benefit subsidy announced yesterday by the Minister of State for Grains after only one year?

subtopic: ELIMINATION OF TWO-PRICE WHEAT SYSTEM-ONE-YEAR ADJUSTMENT PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the Hon. Member is not in possession of the facts when he attempts to make a connection between the phase-out of two-price wheat and the FTA.
I must make it perfectly clear that there is absolutely no connection whatsoever between the Government's decision to phase out the two-price wheat system and the FTA.
The decision was under consideration long before the discussions or negotiations began between the two countries with respect to the FTA. The decision was taken to ensure the financial viability of the Canadian domestic industry.

Mr. Speaker, surely no one believes that the Government is cutting out the two-price wheat system for any other reason than because of the Prime Minister's trade deal with the United States.
What we want to know is how many other agricultural industries, for example, poultry, dairy, or the fruit and vegetable industry will be similarly destroyed? Will they only receive adjustment assistance for one year? Surely the adjustment should be for many years, if the Government is determined to destroy an industry like this, rather than cut it out after only one year.
Is this grant that the Minister announced yesterday just a cynical gimmick because there is an election coming up?

Mr. Speaker, I will try once again and indicate to the House that there is
Oral Questions
absolutely no connection between the phase-out of the two-price wheat system and the FTA.
In respect of the Hon. Member's other reference to the impact of the FTA on Canadian agriculture, the Hon. Member should recognize that that will have very positive effects on Canadian agriculture.
One supplementary?

subsubtopic: PLAN FOR OLD PORT OF QUEBEC-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
My question is directed to the Minister of Public Works and concerns the Old Port in Quebec City. Is the Minister aware of the growing opposition of the people of Quebec City to the Conservative Government's plan for privatizing a substantial part of the Old Port, and more specifically, for the sale of Pointe-a-Carcy to a developer, Rocois Construction?
Since Quebec City has been registered by UNESCO on its world heritage list, why does the Government refuse to say how it will protect the heritage character of this part of the Old Port? Why did it decide to privatize this important location before setting up a plan for the preservation and development of the Old Port?

speakeroldname: Hon. Stewart Mclnnes (Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation
subsubtopic: PLAN FOR OLD PORT OF QUEBEC-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Old Port of Quebec Crown corporation called for proposals for development of the lands in question referred to by the Hon. Member. There were public hearings held over a period of months to give organizations and residents of the area the opportunity to air their views on the pros and cons of the development. After those public hearings were concluded an award was made to one of the developers.
A poll of people in the area indicated that 93 per cent of Quebecers in that area approved of the plan and the development that was eventually chosen.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the President of the Treasury Board. The McLaughlin Report that was released one year ago indicated that the federal Government, through its various Departments and agencies, is one of the largest land holders in Metropolitan Toronto.
I would like to ask the President of the Treasury Board if one of those mysterious arms of the Treasury Board, that is, the Bureau of Real Property Management, would be prepared to release and make available some of that land in Metropolitan Toronto for badly needed housing. Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: THWARTED ATTEMPT TO SMUGGLE ILLEGAL MIGRANTS FROM WEST GERMANY
speechtext:

What action is the Minister taking to prevent and stop the illegal and criminal activities involved in the business of human smuggling?

subsubtopic: THWARTED ATTEMPT TO SMUGGLE ILLEGAL MIGRANTS FROM WEST GERMANY

subsubtopic: CLOSURE OF CERTAIN DISTRIBUTION CENTRES-MINISTER'S POSITION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Communications. The National Film Board's distribution network is gradually disintegrating. subsubtopic: CLOSURE OF CERTAIN DISTRIBUTION CENTRES-MINISTER'S POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will be glad to have a full explanation given to the Hon. Member by the National Film Board. I would like him to understand that what is being put into place is a new system of distribution which will be electronically run and will offer much wider distribution to centres all across Canada than we presently have.
That will mean that there will be some changes to the present system, but it will not mean that there will be any diminution of the services.

PROVISION OF SERVICES IN SMALLER CENTRES
speechtext:

When the Member says that the budget of the National Film Board has been reduced, he might take a look at the
Oral Questions
additional moneys which were just put into film and video distribution. Some $200 million was announced last month and $25 million of that will be going to the National Film Board.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of State for Finance. British Columbia's Alaskan cruise ship industry alleges that it is in danger of being wiped out by the imposition of duties and taxes to which it was not previously subjected. This industry brings in $70 million a year for B.C.'s economy.
Does the Minister know about what is going on out there, and is he doing anything about it?

Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank my hon. friend for his very important question. He knows that in 1987 the cruise industry in British Columbia travelling to Alaska paid no duty or taxes.
I am happy to confirm that it will be paying no duty or excise taxes this year. An interdepartmental committee is examining this whole matter and we hope to put a program in place for the future as well.

In its new corporate plan, Canada Post continues to close rural post offices, it refuses to provide door-to-door mail delivery in new urban developments, but it will continue to increase postal rates by as much as 30 per cent.
Is it true that in March 1988, the Minister recommended that his Cabinet colleagues approve this plan? Was he aware of its contents? And if so, how could he force this kind of injustice on Canadians? Will he withdraw this disastrous plan?

Mr. Chairman, I have a few questions for the Minister. In some cases they are of a fairly broad nature. I waited for the right moment in the Bill to raise these questions, but in order to facilitate the proceedings this afternoon this may be as good a place as any.
First, I wonder if the Minister could give the committee an idea of how much so-called surrendered, or now, more appropriately, designated, land is affected by C-115? I can understand if the Minister does not have it, but perhaps it could be sent along at a later time. I am also interested in what potential revenue this may mean for bands and that information may be in the same category. It may need to be communicated later.
I would also like to have some information from the Minister about the position of the Government of British Columbia regarding Bill C-115. There is a lot of concern about the role of that Government and its relations with Indian people. I am wondering whether, for example, the municipalities of British Columbia have in any way lobbied the Government with respect to this legislation and what has been the effect of that lobbying endeavour on the attitude of the Government of British Columbia.
While we are talking about the province, perhaps the Minister could clarify an issue raised with me over the role of the province in taxing additionally non-Indians on surrendered lands. Is there still a taxation power retained by the province in this regard? I am sorry to throw it all at the Minister at once. I could have done it in a series of questions, but I want to move along as quickly as I can so that we can deal with other Bills related to Indian affairs.
My final question has to do with a concern raised by the Assembly of First Nations. Other chiefs have brought this to my attention as well. Once bands begin to enjoy the revenues from this taxation power being extended to them, is it likely that the Government will use this as a reason for cutting back on what may be described as normal or regular programs? I know the Minister wrote to Chief Georges Erasmus on May 16 and said on the second page, second last paragraph: "Please be assured that it is not the Government's intention to reduce financial support available to non-Indians because of their own tax-raising activities."
I am sure the Minister means what he says and it is not the Government's intention. However, knowing the record of
relations between not only his Government but many Governments over a long period of time with Indian people, sometimes intentions are just not enough. I wonder if there is some way the Minister can strengthen that. Is there some kind of guarantee that First Nations are not going to see cut-backs in normal and regular programs because they have acquired this taxation power?

speakerposition: Minister of the Western Diversification Office; Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
I do not believe it would benefit anyone to provide a guarantee. All Governments need to operate on revenues and grants. Municipal Governments operate on revenues and grants.
I cannot think of a way to guarantee what would be a policy decision. I cannot see the benefit that would arise from such an action by any Government. Indeed, it would discourage Indian Governments from taking the very action that the legislation is allowing them to take, which is long overdue. It allows them to tax their own assets. I cannot see why anyone would want to reduce those revenues.
As I say, all Governments operate on a form of grants and revenues. The revenues that are provided in this case would come from Indian assets. Grants would flow as they do to other forms of government. I do not know how to assure my hon. friend that that could not happen, except that I do not believe it would because it would be totally counter-productive.
He asked if there is the ability for taxation by the province on a non-Indian resident residing on designated land. I believe the answer is yes.
I cannot give him the exact acres with respect to his first question, but there are about 100 bands that have designated lands at this time. We are undertaking to find out how much and what the usage of that land is. I cannot inform the Hon. Member of the outcome of that endeavour at this time.
With respect to how much revenue, I can talk about British Columbia where I believe 60 per cent of the designated lands are located. The revenues on those designated lands are about $5.5 million annually. It is a very small percentage of the municipal revenues in the Province of British Columbia, bearing in mind that there are some municipalities where the proportion of revenue from these lands is much higher than the average in British Columbia.

Mr. Chairman, dealing with the Government's good will in the future regarding regular or normal programs, the Minister is attempting to assure the committee that the kind of thing we mentioned is unlikely to happen, that it is counter-productive. I want very much to believe that.
Of course, the James Bay Cree discovered to their dismay that when they made a settlement with Canada in exchange for vast tracts of land that could then be utilized by the Government of Quebec and Ontario Hydro, they in fact did suffer on certain regular programs. They had to use what were
June 2, 1988

described as compensation funds for community infrastructure.
The Grand Council of the Cree often reported that Indian Affairs officials in the Quebec region told them that since they had done rather well, there is only so much money and the Department had better look after somebody else.
In fact, the Tait Inquiry drew attention to the fact that in many cases they were short-circuited on regular and normal programs because they had made a tripartite agreement with Canada, Quebec and themselves.
Then there is the case in southern Alberta, the Blackfoot cattle claim, where there was an outstanding settlement. When it was decided to negotiate that claim and accept compensation moneys in exchange for cattle, and when the band dispersed those moneys among its members, they found to their dismay that the social assistance was accordingly cut back.
The Minister justified this on the basis that this was the way it was done in the province and he had to follow provincial guidelines.
My point is simply that in the past these kinds of situations have happened. It is easy to understand why bands, in attempting to improve their position, are nervous that there may be some rearguard action that will give on the one hand and take on the other. Therefore, how does one make any progress or get out of the treadmill situation?
The Minister asks me the rhetorical question: What kind of guarantees can be offered? Let me suggest to the Minister that when agreements like this are reached, what is wrong with signing a memorandum of understanding between the Government and the bands that they will in no way be jeopardized in regular or normal programs because they have gained revenue on their own designated lands through taxation?
The Minister admitted that the province will continue to have taxation powers on these designated or formerly called surrendered lands. Will the Minister elaborate and explain to the committee what is the nature of this taxation? What kind of taxation powers are they? Is it a concern of any of the chiefs that these provincial taxation powers will continue?

speakeroldname: Mr. Stan Schellenberger (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it gives me great pleasure today to rise in debate on this Bill, one that my constituents in the constituency of Wetaskiwin have been asking for for some time.
The bands at Hobema use their trust accounts to assist the parents of children to raise minors. This has been the practice of those bands for some time. However, in the last number of years the Auditor General has raised some questions as to the manner in which Parliament is allowing this to take place. So it is indeed a pleasure to see this legislation before us today. Once and for all we will no longer have this practice being questioned by the Auditor General and Members of Parliament as to whether or not it is in fact in order.
One of the primary goals of the Government is to return to Indian people control over their lands, over their lives and over their funds, moneys that have been gathered either through resources, through the Bill which we just finished debating, or in other business activities on the reserve. The manner in which they use those funds should well be within their jurisdiction.
Since coming to office we have moved steadily forward in this regard. We are doing so again with this legislation today. We are giving new impetus to the whole area of devolution, encouraging local decision-making and Indian participation in the development and delivery of a wide range of programs.

June 2, 1988
Indian Act
The Bill before us today is an important step for all Indian people. The key element of Bill C-123 is that it will provide Indian bands with an opportunity to take an active role in the release of funds to Indian minors, to parents or guardians of such minors, which is presently the sole responsibility of the Minister.
Indian people have the ability to direct their affairs and those of their children. The legislation before us today is very progressive in that sense. In fact, it has been in practice for some time.
As I have said before, serious concerns have been raised by the Auditor General concerning the way that the Department discharges its trust responsibilities. Accordingly, many of those concerns are now being addressed through a major review of the Department's plans, revenues and trust functions. As a result, this Bill, Bill C-123, deals almost exclusively with minors' trust funds.
Presently under the Indian Act all moneys derived from the sale or lease of Indian lands and resources are held in trust by the Government of Canada for use by the bands. As well, the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. McKnight) is authorized to direct the expenditure of those funds for the benefit of the bands concerned.
The Indian Act also authorizes him, with the consent of a band, to arrange payments to individuals or individual band members. The total amount distributed in this way cannot exceed 50 per cent of the band's capital moneys derived from the sale of surrendered lands. These lands are generally surrendered for resource exploration purposes.
Distribution payments to minors are held by the Government of Canada in individual trust accounts and released to minors when they reach the age of majority. The Department now maintains about 19,000 of these accounts worth more than $145 million. The vast majority are held on behalf of resource-rich bands in Alberta, or other bands of a resource nature in British Columbia.
One of the difficulties that I have noted over the years with respect to holding trust accounts until the age of majority, particularly in the oil-producing bands of Alberta, is that when these funds are released to a person who reaches 18 years of age there is a great feeling that these young people are not yet capable of investing, in some cases many tens of thousands of dollars, at that age. They often use that money to their personal detriment. Perhaps they buy a new car, which we are all susceptible to doing when we receive some money, and then go out on a bit of a celebration because of the windfall that comes at 18 years of age. I have spoken to the chiefs about this issue, and together we should consider a way in which this money can be sent out to the person after the age of majority, not all at once but in payments over a period of a number of years. That is an aside, but is relevant to what is happening and to this Bill.
In 1981, Indian bands in Alberta asked the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development to make payments from these trust funds to parents or guardians of Indian minors to help provide for minors. A departmental directive was subsequently developed, and has been used for the last five years. Upon receipt of a band council resolution, the Department will pay up to $3,000 annually from the distribution made on behalf of minor band members directly to the parents or guardians of all such minors, in the band.
However, there are no specific provisions in the Indian Act authorizing the Minister to make payments to parents or guardians of minors, on a minor's behalf without a specific request for that money, and also establishing the need for that money. The Auditor General has suggested that the Minister is bound by provincial trust laws, common law practices and principles of trust.
Bill C-123 is designed to incorporate the basic principles of the provincial regimes governing moneys held on behalf of all minors in Canada, while still accommodating the particular needs and circumstances of Indian minors. In this manner, it strikes an important balance between ensuring that Indian communities can protect the interests of their minors, and providing for the lawful release of moneys by the Government of Canada to those who are entitled to them.
Specifically, Bill C-123 amends the Indian Act to provide the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development with express discretionary authority to make payments from a minor's trust fund to a parent or guardian for the maintenance, advancement, or benefit of the minor.
The legislation further amends the Indian Act to provide band councils with the authority to direct the Minister to pay all or part of per capita distributions owed to an Indian minor to a parent, guardian, or the council for the minor's maintenance, advancement, or other benefit. Under this amendment, the council itself may assume responsibility for distribution to a parent or guardian. The amount payable will be the lesser of $3,000, or the amount of the annual per capita distribution paid to members of the band.
Bill C-123 also amends the Indian Act to enable the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development to pay all moneys owing to the minor at age of majority in a series of payments over a period of not more than three years. This is what I mentioned before, Mr. Speaker. In some cases, perhaps three years is not long enough, but it certainly is an improvement over what was allowed in the past.
A request to make payments in this way must be made in writing to the Minister by a parent, guardian, or the council of the band to which the minor belongs. This provision was included at the request of concerned Indian parents who were becoming increasingly alarmed at the tragic loss of their children's heritage through their inability to manage large sums of money at the age of majority.
June 2, 1988

These amendments are important from both a legal and a practical point of view. From a legal standpoint, they ensure that the Minister has the authority to discharge his trust responsibilities. From a practical standpoint, they ensure that at least some of the minor's trust money is available for his or her maintenance, advancement, or benefit.
The Bill also provides for one other important amendment to the Indian Act. This one is unrelated to minors' trust funds. Subsections 48(1) and 48(2) of the Indian Act will be amended to increase a surviving spouse's preferential share in the estate of an intestate from $2,000 to $75,000. This brings the Indian Act in line with the most progressive provincial legislation in this area.
Progress, fairness, and keeping commitments are what this Bill is all about. I know that all Members from all Parties are concerned about this, and hopefully this Bill can be moved along relatively quickly.

The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. McKnight that Bill C-123, an Act to amend the Indian Act (minors' funds and surviving spouse's preferential share), be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.

Mr. Speaker, this is not an extraordinarily complicated piece of legislation, by any means. It simply clarifies the Minister's trust responsibilities for moneys held by Canada on behalf of an Indian person who has not yet reached the age of majority.
The Bill amends the Indian Act to provide the Minister with express authority, as indicated by the Parliamentary Secretary, to make payments to those who have not reached the age of
Indian Act
majority on the request of a parent, guardian, or the band council in order that a child's maintenance and advancement or other benefit may be looked after.
Anyone tuning into this debate may wonder why it is that we are amending the Indian Act, and why it is necessary for us to do so. The answer is that in 1986 the Auditor General raised concerns about the trust accounts for Indian children held by the Government of Canada. They are called the minors' trust accounts. As the law now reads, the Minister of Indian Affairs must maintain trust accounts for Indian children until they reach the age of majority.
This is all part of what I consider to be the outdated but still lingering paternalism in this country which still characterizes the relationship between the Government of Canada and Indian people generally. I cannot imagine any other Canadian allowing such interference by the state in his or her personal financial matters and concerns.
Did you know, Mr. Speaker, that, pursuant to the Indian Oil and Gas Act, all the royalties from oil and gas reserves held by Indians and that come from Indian lands are held in trust by the federal Government on behalf of the bands concerned. I do not know what message that communicates to you or to my colleagues in the House, but to me the underlying supposition is that somehow these bands cannot, by themselves, be trusted to handle and disburse their own revenues. That flies in the face of self-determination, to which I will return in a moment.
Trust accounts for minors must be held by the Government until they reach the age of majority. There are some 14,000 such trust accounts at present, with a value of approximately $100 million. Despite the obligation to hold these moneys until the child reaches the age of maturity, it has in the past been the Department's practice to release annually around $3,000 on request for a child's education, maintenance, or benefit. That is to say, this money could be released to the child's parent or guardian.
Here comes the rub. There is fear about the Minister's liability in doing this. That is to say, the Minister might at some time in the future be sued for breach of trust by an Indian person whose trust moneys were disbursed while he or she was still a minor.
We have to be very frank in this House of Commons that what we are doing this afternoon with Bill C-123 is not something for Indian people, despite what the Parliamentary Secretary would like us to believe. What we are doing this afternoon is something to protect the Minister. We are trying to keep the Minister from being sued for breach of trust.
The Auditor General noted that in order to make these payments from a minor's trust account there really ought to be, according to the various trust acts in the provinces, a court order. Obviously, every time $3,000 was granted to a parent or guardian the Department of Indian Affairs did not want to get

June 2, 1988
Indian Act
a court order. That would be a bureaucratic nightmare. If we do not want to go the court route, Section 52 of the Indian Act must be amended to give express authority to the Minister to advance such trust funds for the maintenance and education of Indian minors. That is what we are doing with Bill C-123. Therefore, this is a simple Bill to help out the Minister and his successors.
However, this problem of liability does not just dissipate and go away. We have transferred liability from the Minister to the band council. Band councils which make a determination that money is needed and request the disbursement of funds for a particular child themselves become liable and may find themselves at some time in a breach of trust situation.
Neither I nor my Party want to stand in the way of this Bill in any way. We will not hold it up at all. We want the Minister to have the protection he is seeking. As long as the Government of Canada has the enormous power and control, which is almost totalitarian in scope, over Indian people, a Bill like C-123 will be necessary.
It ought to be demonstrated through this legislation to Members of the House and all Canadians just how far we in Canada still are from recognizing the right to self-determination of Indian people. The failure to recognize the inherent right of aboriginal people to self-government in our Constitution continues, day after day, year after year, to compound our problems.
The sad thing is that we came so close. We almost made a breakthrough. We stood at the very edge of a major decision to complete the Canadian federation by inviting aboriginal people to come in, not as wards of the state, but as partners of our Confederation. However, at the last minute at the last of those First Ministers' Conferences there was a hesitation. I do not at all place all the blame on the present administration. There was provincial hesitation as well-hesitation and withdrawal. The political will failed. The vision which was seen for a moment faded and courage folded.
We are now at the point where a new generation of Indian leaders is rapidly losing patience. I have marveled, in the many years in which I have been involved in the House of Commons with aboriginal affairs and Indian rights, at the degree of patience which has existed among the leadership of the aboriginal communities. However, Chief Erasmus in Edmonton this week alluded to the fact that that patience is beginning to dry up, it is beginning to run out.
I raise this in the House of Commons because I think Members of Parliament from every political Party ought to be concerned. I do not believe that Chief Erasmus was threatening anyone, I do not believe he was sabre rattling. I think he was simply reporting on a reality which is becoming more and more apparent to him. The situation in Canada is deteriorating and statesmen like Georges Erasmus may not be able to control the situation unless they get co-operation and understanding from members of the administration and all Members of Parliament.
In his book written in 1976, I believe, entitled Across the Medicine Line, C. Frank Turner quotes Sitting Bull, Chief of the Sioux, who at one time explained to Inspector Walsh of the Northwest Mounted Police why he had left the United States of America to enter Canada, which he did in the year 1876. Sitting Bull said: "The grass in Canada is not stained with blood".
Members of the House may know that the civil rights activist Rap Brown once said that violence in the United States is as American as cherry pie. Well, that is not the tradition in Canada and it must never become the route to problem solving. Violent action is always, inevitably, a no-win situation for everyone. If anyone doubts that, all they need do is to look at Beirut or Belfast.
There exists in Canada today the most vital need to establish a new working relationship between aboriginal peoples and the Government of Canada. This new relationship must be established on two pillars, the first being the full recognition of aboriginal rights, including that of self-determination. The second pillar is fair, honest, and open negotiating in order to settle and resolve differences, disputes, and problems.
Until this is done we are going to go on and on tinkering with the Indian Act. We will continue to see matters like the Lubicon claim in northern Alberta mushroom into an international issue. We are going to continue to see police raids such as the one on the Kahnawake Reserve on the Mohawk people where, I am told, some 200 RCMP officers in three buses descended with loaded automatic rifles. Why? Because there is a problem there, a dispute, a misunderstanding, about the importation of cigarettes and the taxation of those cigarettes as they are sold. It seems to me that a problem like that can be resolved if reasonable people sit down around the table to try to solve it. In fact, I am advised that negotiations were in progress at Kahnawake on this matter.
I ask the House and the Government, where are we going when we send in 200 police officers with loaded automatic rifles to solve a problem like that? This is not the Canada that I thought we lived in. It seems to me when we do things like that we are on the very verge of becoming some kind of police state. It is time to call off that kind of action and proceed in a totally different way. Until we do, Mr. Speaker, there will be more and more grievances. The list will get longer and longer and the situation will become increasingly more tragic. This does not have to happen. There is a reasonable, informed, talented and capable leadership with the aboriginal communities of this country, but it does not feel that it has access to problem solving. The leadership feels that it is being manipulated, pushed around and used.
I am asking Parliament and the Government of Canada, for God's sake come to your senses and stop. What we need here in Ottawa is the kind of political leadership which is strong enough to say that the kind of paternalism that has gone on in
June 2, 1988

this country for so long has to come to an end. Confrontation has to stop whether it is between police officers and band members or whether that confrontation is in a court of law. Why can matters not be resolved by way of negotiation? No finer a Canadian than the Hon. E. Davie Fulton said that the problem at Lubicon could be resolved. He gave a recipe for the resolution and he agreed to become the mediator. His recipe, his plan and volunteering to be a mediator were all rejected. The Minister decided instead to throw the whole issue into a court of law based on well defined premises laid down ahead of time by the Government of Canada. It is not the way to proceed, Mr. Speaker. It will not work. It will simply compound our problem.
I thank you, Sir, for your patience, but I want to make a plea once again. We have to begin today to establish a new working relationship with the aboriginal people of this country, a relationship between the Government of Canada and the aboriginal people, a relationship that will work, will yield understanding and goodwill, rather than have the situation that we see at present.

Mr. Speaker, as my friend just said, Bill C-123 will do what it is designed for. It is a legal bandage for the Minister and for the Department of Indian and Northern Affairs.
I had an interesting conversation earlier this week with some senior people from the Department regarding the five Bills we are dealing with today. I was not shocked but I was not amused to hear from them. I am not sure what code names they use. People who are senior in the Department use code names now. The one I am speaking of is probably "S", although I am not sure. I know he is probably watching the debate. I was not amused to learn that there is extensive, widespread law-breaking taking place right now by the Department in relation to the very issue before us today. It has been going on for many years and at great length. It was a point finally driven home, I suppose, by the Auditor General.
As is often the case in aboriginal matters in this country in recent years, matters seem to be resolved, at least in part, in the interests of Canada's first citizens by rulings by the United Nations as we saw in the Lovelace case, and ultimately by Bill C-131, which I said yesterday is like a balloon that has been heavily perforated with all kinds of legal problems.
The five Bills we have before us today I described earlier as being the good, the bad and the ugly. The ugly Bill C-122 we dealt with just before lunch. It deals with changes proposed by the Government to by-laws and the procedures affecting bylaws. This one I describe as bad. My friend, the Hon. Member for Cochrane-Superior (Mr. Penner) touched on some of the reasons why many Canadians and Members of Parliament consider this kind of an approach to be bad. Where is the commitment to self-government when one looks at Bill C-123? Where is the consultation? Where is the imagination in dealing with what I was advised about yesterday in terms of the total? The minors' trust is about $100 million, but if you
Indian Act
look at the total amount being held by the Government of Canada, it is around $900 million. Where is the imagination to deal with funds of this amount? They are sitting in the Consolidated Revenue Fund drawing interest the same as a Treasury bill. There are sufficient funds to do all kinds of things in terms of leverage, banking proposals, in setting up tourist industries et cetera. Where is the imagination? There is no imagination in this Bill. All it is is a big roll of Elastoplast bandage to protect the Minister from being sued, from being in court, from having his bureaucrats charged with all kinds of offences. The officials admitted to me the day before yesterday that there is rampant law-breaking going on, and I am talking about very senior officials in the Department.
My friend from Cochrane-Superior asked, how does the Government respond to a treaty issue under negotiations at Kahnawake with the federal Government? How has it responded there? A para-military troop of 200 police officers has gone in with machine guns. This is the importation of violence. Whoever in Canada made this decision must have been watching Rambo I, Rambo II and Rambo III back to back a little too much lately. That is violence, Mr. Speaker. That is violent activity by the state against a group of peaceful people who have been operating this kind of a commercial transaction for years in full view. It is not hidden. It is not some kind of underground operation. The federal Government should hang its head in shame for the way it has been responding to this issue here in the House and outside in the last 48 hours.
The Auditor General in 1986 asked certain questions about whether or not the Minister had the authority to make payments out of trust funds for minors. The second part of this Bill is the distribution of estates, a problem that has been chronic in some cases. I do not know any other identifiable group in Canadian society that has had to put up with such things. Some payments in relation to estates have been held up for 20 years under the existing bureaucratic regime set up by the Department.
I talked earlier today about the kind of political pulp that comes out of the Minister's office every once in a while on Bills like Bills C-122, C-123 and others. It is basically propaganda trying to paint a nice face on legislation that is coming forward. Here is how it was covered by the press:
The federal government has set out rules to ensure Indian bands, parents or guardians don't raid trust accounts set up for young native people.
That is a nice way to put it. It continues:
Under a bill tabled in the Commons this week, a band council would have to give 14 days notice that it intends to take money out of a minor's trust account, and would have to hear any objections from band members at a general meeting.
Withdrawals would be limited to $3,000 a year and would have to be used only for the benefit of the child, such as paying education expenses.
Guardians who want to get at the cash would have to apply directly to the Indian Affairs minister, stating in writing how the money will benefit the minor. There would be no cash limit on the amount the Minister can approve.

June 2, 1988
Indian Lands Agreement (1986) Act
What is this Parliament up to? This kind of paternalistic attitude, I suppose, is best revealed. I do not think it is a political philosophy per se, I think it is an attitude, perhaps most rampantly and repugnantly revealed in the remarks of someone who is in Cabinet in British Columbia. Stephen Rogers, when he was commenting on South Moresby, said, "Wouldn't it be wonderful, the Haidas could act as so-called living exhibits in South Moresby". There is a revelation by someone in Cabinet thinking, "Aboriginal people. They will attract tourists. We will have them as living exhibits in South Moresby". This is a living exhibit of the same kind of mentality. It is not an attempt to deal realistically with extensive sums of money that should be flowing more appropriately to settle estates of someone whose spouse passes away. Right now one can get $2,000 automatically, and here in Ontario, there is a case of a family that has been waiting 20 years for the Department to settle the estate. That is preposterous. I am not sure that this Bill will speed things up.
Let me carry on with this story:
The accounts, for which the minister is a trustee, are created when a share of royalties from oil and gas revenues on Indian lands must be distributed to band members younger than 18 years.
The federal spending watchdog, Auditor General Ken Dye, criticized the department in his 1986 report for automatically releasing $3,000 a year from all minors' trust accounts without the written request of the parent or guardian and regardless of need.
The Minister has been automatically releasing funds without any justification as to whether the minor needs it or not or whether it is ever spent on a hockey glove, a bus pass to get to school or the fee to join an orchestra. What is proposed here is nothing better.
If we are to really move toward self-government, and I think the will to do so exists in Canada and, if properly mobilized, even exists here in this Chamber, we should close down the Department of Indian Affairs. This Bill sets up a whole new bureaucracy. As quick as we can rub one out, another one is built, another great dream castle to deal paternalistically with those people.
Of course, this violates laws. As I said, senior bureaucrats admit that there is widespread law-breaking going on, but I do not see any charges being laid by the Solicitor General (Mr. Kelleher) or by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Hnatyshyn). Perhaps that is the way this should have been dealt with, rather than with this legal Elastoplast.
The publication continues:
And an 11-page legal opinion for the department by University of Victoria law professor Donovan Waters warned that the current system violates provincial trust laws and should be changed.
We did not hear from the Parliamentary Secretary or from the Minister yet whether or not that will continue to be the case. Obviously, this is a good reason why this piece of legislation should go to a legislative committee for proper hearings. To continue:
The opinion-argued that no money should be released without evidence of need.
The bill, an amendment to the Indian Act, aims also to cut into the backlog of cases involving the distribution of the estates of deceased natives.
Dye's 1986 report noted long delays in the department's handling of estates, partly because of poor staff training. In Ontario alone, there were about 600 such cases awaiting settlement, some of them more than 20 years old.
Under the proposed legislation, up to $75,000 from an estate could be automatically given to the surviving spouse. The current limit for automatic payment is $2,000.
Departmental officials and Dye agreed in 1986 that the higher limit would reduce the estate-settlement workload.
A spokesman for the Assembly of First Nations said the bill was put together without consulting native groups and that it barely touches the huge financial mismanagement problem at the department.
"They got stung so they're scratching in one spot, ignoring the rash on the other side of the body," Ted Montour said Thursday.
I will not spend any more time on this Bill. I am looking forward to getting it before the legislative committee. I do not know that we can amend it in the direction of the principle that should have driven it, the principle of self-government and providing control of trust funds with those they are for. Surely that should be an underlying principle that all parliamentarians could agree on. I do not think there is a Member of this House who would agree to this kind of a Bill which would affect his or her children, grandchildren, cousins, nephews, nieces, uncles, aunts, fathers or mothers.
As I said earlier, this Bill falls into today's category of bad legislation. It is not ugly like the one with which we dealt a little earlier nor is it good like two of the ones with which we have already dealt today.
Is the House ready for the question?
Question.
Is it the pleasure of the House to adopt the motion?
Agreed.
Motion agreed to, Bill read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.

speakerposition: Minister of the Western Diversification Office; Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subtopic: INDIAN LANDS AGREEMENT (1986) ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I hope it will not be necessary, but I very much appreciate it.
Bill C-73, the Indian Lands Agreement (1986) Act, basically brings into play discussions that have gone on for several years regarding Indian lands in Ontario. It will provide a mechanism to resolve the question of control over unsold surrendered Indian lands and the royalties derived from mineral rights that are now being held.
By providing for a means to negotiate these issues, the 1986 Indian Lands Agreement could lead to the return of unsold surrendered lands to Ontario Indians and to their full entitlement to the mineral royalties on reserve lands. This will in turn contribute to the economic development in some communities and to the establishment of infrastructure that is indeed needed to support Indian Government.
The Governments of Canada and Ontario attempted to resolve a series of post-Confederation court decisions which established that title to surrendered Indian lands and the mineral resources on them be passed to the provincial Government. Among other things, these decisions cast doubt on the legality of past federal sales of surrendered Indian lands. This situation occurred in 1984, and the agreements were designed to give the federal Government the right to sell surrendered lands and to transfer the proceeds to the appropriate bands.
Despite the good intentions, the agreement was ambiguous in wording and brought into question whether it applied to lands surrendered before the agreement was signed. Moreover, under the 1924 agreement, Ontario retains 50 per cent of all mineral royalties on the lands.
As a result of this ambiguity, several million dollars in royalties are now being held in suspense accounts. Efforts have been ongoing since the late 1950s to resolve the problems that were found in the 1924 agreement. It was not until March, 1986 when the Indian Lands Agreement was approved by the Ontario tripartite council of federal and provincial Ministers and Indian association leaders that the agreement we are talking about today was finally reached.
Naturally, there are two sides to this. The 1924 agreement was ratified by Parliament and by the provincial legislature, and further legislation is required to amend the terms and conditions. On the federal side, that legislation is Bill C-73.
Indian Lands Agreement (1986) Act
Similar enacting legislation will have to be introduced in the Ontario Legislature.
The Indian Lands Agreement (1986) will allow the federal and Ontario Governments and individual Indian bands to negotiate specific agreements regarding the future control of the lands and minerals in question. It confirmed the federal Government's right to retain and administer land sale revenues for Indian bands.
In Ontario there are some 2.5 million acres of reserve land which has been surrendered by Indian bands. Not all of it has been sold. With the passage of this important legislation, the reserve land base of Ontario will have a potential to increase by as much as 12 per cent or 200,000 acres. We also anticipate that as part of specific agreements Ontario will relinquish its interest in existing mineral royalties which are now being held in suspense. Those royalties are worth today some $4.3 million.
The future value of mineral rights is, I think, even more important. Over the next 15 years royalties which could be worth several millions of dollars will flow to the bands in question. There is also provision for a separate agreement to ratify federal letters patent, some 33,000 of which have been issued to non-Indians for title to Indian lands. As I say, the expanded land and resource base resulting from this Bill will contribute to economic development in Ontario.
The impact will be favourable on a number of Indian bands in Ontario. Some 30 bands will eventually be involved in negotiations arising out of Bill C-73. Sixteen bands have already started the process. An example is the Nipissing Band which is negotiating agreements involving some 34,000 acres and Sarnia, which is negotiating for royalties of some $4.3 million now being held in trust, and six bands are involved in negotiations for the land at Manitoulin Island.
As we go forward we are prepared to assist Indian bands as much as possible during this negotiating process. My Department will be offering financial assistance to bands who undertake these negotiations. I would like to assure Hon. Members that this Act will in no way prejudice Indian rights in Ontario. In fact, I believe it will advance those rights by providing Indian people with a greatly enhanced opportunity for economic development. Neither will this Act affect third parties. I believe that as we look to where occupied lands cannot be returned to reserve status, other methods of compensation must be explored.
In conclusion, there are two features which have to be stressed. It is important to note that the agreement is between the Governments of Canada and Ontario, but there is strong support from most Indian bands in Ontario. I think that reflects a commitment by all three parties to resolve a longstanding issue so that the development of Indian lands and resources can proceed.

June 2, 1988
Indian Lands Agreement (1986) Act
The second point is that the lands agreement is an opting-in agreement. That means the bands who do not wish to enter into any specific agreement will continue to be governed by the 1924 agreement. This is in keeping with the policy of proceeding with changes according to the timetable of Indian bands.
I want to point out that there are many bands in Ontario who are eager to proceed quickly with Bill C-73 so that they can accelerate the vital task of economic development for bands in Ontario. As we proceed we will both be able to clarify an outstanding problem and again benefit all people in Ontario by causing economic development to take place.

subtopic: INDIAN LANDS AGREEMENT (1986) ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank my hon. friend from Cochrane-Superior and also the Minister for keeping his remarks brief so that I can get into the air to British Columbia.
Bill C-73 is supported by most groups in Ontario, so I am advised. I also understand there are some who are opposed to it and I can understand why they might well be. However, I think by having this legislation go from here to a legislative committee an opportunity will be open for the chiefs of Ontario who have requested that the legislation be studied in committee to make their views known, as will groups such as the Association of Iroquois and Allied Indians who have expressed concerns about the legislation. They will be able to air their views once it is in committee.
The one point I do not think can be passed by today is that we have to send a signal to the Legislature at Queen's Park in Toronto that they must reintroduce the parallel legislation that was before their Chamber two years ago but lapsed after the Legislature was dissolved. It has not been reintroduced. The fact we are dealing with it today in an expeditious manner may well be a sufficient signal. However, it may well be that Members participating in this debate and who are concerned about this issue will have to take additional steps to get the Government of Ontario to move to bring in the parallel legislation necessary to implement the tripartite process we are moving on today.
The problem is an old one. It started in 1867 with respect to most of the land. In fact, just 100 years ago, in 1888, there was the famed St. Catharines Milling case, which of course is part and parcel of what we are dealing with here today. It involves about 30,000 properties, if one were to look at the individual titles in Ontario with letters patent from the federal Government, but letters patent that are not really what one could describe as full title or title in fee simple. There are technical legal problems with how the land was ceded, and that is in part what we will be dealing with in Bill C-73.
About 200,000 acres are affected. Sixteen bands have expressed direct interest in proceeding and, as the Minister said, and I am sure my friend from Cochrane-Superior will
restate, it is certainly our view from reading this legislation that it is an opt-in situation. Those who wish to stay outside of this process can continue to operate under the 1924 lands agreement.
It is a situation somewhat different from that in my home Province of British Columbia. We have only 14 very small treaty areas on Vancouver Island that were dealt with wisely by Governor Douglas a long time ago, and Treaty 8 in the northwest part of the province. The matter of land and a land base in Ontario is somewhat more complicated, to say the least. There is not what one could describe as the comprehensive claims settlement process that will ultimately deal with the land question of British Columbia. It is more a situation of specific claims.
Sadly, there are now almost 500 specific claims backed up in Canada, many of them here in Ontario, and only a few of them can be dealt with by the passage of Bill C-73 as it stands or as it may well be amended in the legislative committee when it goes there after today's debate. Therefore, I look forward to having this go through second reading today.
I know there are some in the country, as I said earlier, and some in Ontario, some first citizens and First Nations, who oppose this kind of approach to dealing with individual parcels of land. Certain people have a very much different relationship to land per se than do many other cultures and civilizations. However, I think at least in a small way, perhaps somewhat like Bill C-115 which we dealt with earlier today, this is a tool that will be effective and valuable to some bands and some individuals who will be able to make use of it once it passes through here and in a parallel fashion through the provincial Legislature in Ontario so we can get on with the process of returning at least those 200,000 acres which have been tied up in this rather bizarre legal problem with respect to deeding and patenting of the land.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it should be understood by anyone observing this debate on Bill C-73 that, strictly speaking, we are not legislating anything. Through Bill C-73 we are ratifying an agreement that has already been reached. This Bill implements an agreement respecting Indian lands in Ontario. The purpose of Bill C-73 is to confirm and ratify a bilateral agreement between Canada and Ontario.
That agreement is known as the 1986 Indian Lands Agreement. That agreement is appended to the Bill as a schedule.
While the 1986 agreement came close to being ratified by the Legislature of Ontario, an election interfered and we are still waiting for the Legislature to ratify the agreement. However, we are ratifying the agreement in the House of Commons this afternoon.
June 2, 1988

The agreement to which I am referring makes it possible for three parties-Canada, Ontario and any Indian band or group of bands-to negotiate regarding certain lands and resources in Ontario.
These lands became alienated from the Indian people at some point and passed over to the Province of Ontario as a result of an earlier agreement between Canada and Ontario that was signed in 1924. This agreement passed over to the Province of Ontario complete beneficial interest in any surrendered Indian land and any federal Government control or administration of those lands seized.
Furthermore, under that 1924 agreement, Ontario was able to retain 50 per cent of all mineral royalties arising from the sale of minerals underlying those Indian lands.
It must be clear for those who follow such matters that Bill C-73 is not altering the 1924 agreement at all. It is providing for three-party negotiations regarding land and natural resources that have become an issue through this process of alienation.
The Minister has already given us the figures. We are talking about some possible 200,000 acres which could be added to the reserve land base of Ontario Indians. It may never happen, but it is possible that that much land could be at stake. As well, through these negotiations, the province may in time relinquish its interests in Indian mineral royalties, and these royalties are potentially worth many millions of dollars.
It has to be understood by the House that there is no guarantee that this land and these royalties will in fact be returned. A procedure will be put in place whereby these lands and these resources may be obtained if the negotiations are successful and if there is a settlement. However, there can be no settlement until we ratify the agreement of 1986. That is what we are doing now.
The Minister mentioned that there has already been one settlement, the Nipissing Band. As soon as the agreement is ratified they are in a position to receive some 34,000 acres. The Sarnia Band could receive something close to $5 million, which is Ontario's share of revenues from the sale of minerals underlying the Sarnia reserve.
Again, my colleague, the Member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton), and the Minister both mentioned that there are another 16 bands in Ontario who are seeking to obtain specific agreements.
I repeat that no agreement can become effective until this Parliament and the provincial Legislature of Ontario complete the ratification process.
There is some opposition to the 1986 agreement between Canada and Ontario by some Indian leaders in Ontario. There are some who object to the idea that they have to negotiate with the provincial jurisdiction regarding Indian land and mineral rights.
Indian Lands Agreement (1986) Act
I want people to try to grasp a principle that is strongly held by many Indian leaders. The principle to which they hold dearly is that when they relate to the Crown, that Crown is with the federal Government and not with the provincial authorities. Therefore, many Indian leaders insist that the relationship always remain bilateral in nature and that negotiations be bilateral negotiations.
It has also come to my attention that Ontario is insisting that any renegotiation of the 1924 agreement has to be done on a quid pro quo basis. I have not been able to get more information about that, but I have carefully examined the agreement which is part of the schedule and I do not see that there.
When the Bill goes to the legislative committee we will have to look very carefully at what Ontario means when it talks about renegotiating on a quid pro quo basis. There are certain chiefs in Ontario, with whom I agree, who find it unacceptable and highly objectionable to be called upon to give up something in return for the correction of a past injustice. That would make no sense at all.
If that does somehow reside in the agreement that we are now ratifying, we will have to be sure that we take it out and make the negotiations open and clean and that no such prerequisite is established.
Bill C-73 basically provides nothing more than a legal framework to allow negotiations with the province to get under way. No Indian band is obliged to negotiate. Where negotiations do occur, leading to agreement, there is another aspect of the Bill which will have to be studied at the clause by clause stage. There is a clause that carries with it the tones of the old extinguishment problem that we have in our land claims process at the present time.
Members will want to look carefully at Clause 6 which says that all existing and future members of any band, and the council of that band and all its successors, are bound for all time by any such agreement that is negotiated. It is a very binding agreement on the band members and the band council.
Is it not strange that there is no such binding obligation imposed upon the federal or provincial Governments which enter into this agreement? The Government is insisting that this clause be there to prevent any future legal obligations, but what is there in the agreement to prevent the Government of Canada or the Government of Ontario from reneging on its obligations? There is nothing there at all.
Of course, if one wanted to write the history of Canada from the perspective of Indian people, it would be a history of reneging on agreements, of breaking promises, ignoring treaties, of backing away from obligations and trampling on rights. That is a history that is not taught in the schools. It is a history that is known by some but not widely dispersed by way of textbooks.
There is some controversy about Bill C-73 among Indian leaders in Ontario. These differences of opinion must be aired

Patients' Rights
when Bill C-73 goes before the legislative committee. Perhaps in some respects we may be able to satisfy all the parties if appropriate amendments are introduced to allay concerns about the Bill and its effect. If that is the case, I ask the Minister if he would be willing to co-operate with the legislative committee if we want to make necessary changes based on the testimony we will receive? I conclude on a note about parliamentary reform. The Hon. James McGrath served this Parliament so well by establishing through his report that legislative and standing committees ought to be a check, a balance, against the powers of the executive and the administration and they ought to be able to exercise their authority based on testimony, consensus and agreement. So far these reforms are in the letter but have yet to be realized in the Parliament of Canada fully in their spirit.
