subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   HEALTH SUGGESTED DEVELOPMENT OF POLICIES ON PATIENTS' RIGHTS
PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   HEALTH SUGGESTED DEVELOPMENT OF POLICIES ON PATIENTS' RIGHTS
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of participating with the provinces in the consideration and development of policies in the field of patients' rights, including the right of patients to have access to their files and the obligation for doctors and hospitals to keep patients' records for at least fifty years, and to encourage the enactment of provincial legislation on such matters.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to make a few comments in support of my Motion 114 relating to the question of patients' rights to access to their medical records and their rights to have those records retained by doctors and hospitals.
The issue of patients' rights was first brought to my attention by a constituent's letter a year ago. Since then I have written to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) a number of times, and I have raised it in statements in the House of Commons. What this motion does is to urge the federal Government to work with the provinces to try to implement a scheme by which patients' rights would be recognized, including the right to have access to their files, and to have their records retained for a period of up to 50 years be enshrined in legislation.
I am sure all Members, after they have had an opportunity to think about the issue and have had a chance to look at the facts, will want to agree with the principle. I hope we will have agreement on this motion so it can be referred to the Standing Committee on National Health and Welfare for study. The problem, of course, is not with the principle but rather with the implementation. I think an hour is plenty of time for this House to agree on the principle involved, but it will take officials from the federal, provincial and territorial Governments many hours, indeed, days, weeks and months, to agree on some process for implementation. It is something like the federal Government trying to get 13 clocks of different brands all ticking at the same rate.
I want to say a word of appreciation to Ruth McVeigh, my research assistant, for initiative and hard work in developing this issue, for contacting the provinces and getting information from them. The need for patients to have access to their own files was shown by a letter sent by a constituent-who first raised this matter with me-to the Minister of Health in British Columbia, the Hon. Peter Dueck. I would like to read extensively from that letter. It says:
Dear Mr. Dueck:
As you may be aware there are currently actions being taken against the A.H. Robins Company due to damages caused by their I.U.D. Daikon Shield, which was fitted in many women in Canada in the early 1970s. These damages include infections, infertility, septic abortions and deaths.
My wife was fitted with a Daikon Shield in 1974 in Montreal, Quebec. Many of the records concerning the fitting, and subsequent hospitalization due to complications were lost or destroyed between then and 1985 when we first tried to get these records. Acquiring the hospital records that were left took several letters, phone calls, and ultimately a trip to Montreal. This proved frustrating and time consuming, but we were finally able to acquire some records while keeping costs below $ 100.
Recently my wife's law firm requested proof of the surgery and other treatment she had recently with her current OB/GYN here in Victoria. These treatments relate to the damages the I.U.D. caused. When she went to see her OB/GYN about getting copies of her medical records, she was informed by her OB/GYN that he would not release the records to her, and in fact would not release the records to her lawyers either without a payment of $222 plus photocopying and postal costs. Although the law firm representing her offered to pay for medical record fees from her award settlement, her OB/GYN refused to provide a copy of her records unless he was prepaid.
This has created quite a snag in our case. Neither my wife nor I can afford the kind of fees for medical records being requested. We are working with the lawyers on contingency because we cannot afford to hire a lawyer at salary. Also, there is the possibility the courts may request another copy of her medical records directly from her OB/GYN, new records may be needed to update the file at a later date if the case continues to be delayed (it has already taken 2 years), and my case is separate from my wife's, which may mean I need separate copies of the records. This could end up costing over a thousand dollars just for the file from one of her doctors. Also, after all these costs my wife still would not have a copy of the records to review for accuracy. There is a possibility that errors exist in her file, since she speaks with a strong accent...
June 2, 1988

There is even a greater issue at stake in this matter. As I understand it, the B.C. Medical Plan pays doctors for the time it takes them to write up the original medical record (as part of the office visit fee), the plan pays for the diagnostic lab reports and tests, the plan pays for hospital and surgical reports, and so forth. The discretionary $222 fee (plus photocopying fees) the B.C. Medical Association suggests be charged to patients for the service of sending a copy of medical records to lawyers, insurance companies or others is actually a type of double billing since most of the time involved in creating the original medical record has already been paid for by the B.C. Medical Plan. Doctors regularly provide this copying of medical records and summary sheet to other doctors as a professional courtesy, free of charge. Obviously, the time involved is not that great. My G.P., who believes patients have the right to retain copies of their medical records, often provides me with copies of my records for the cost of photocopying. This $222 charge suggested by the B.C. Medical Association to its members is a bit like going to a car mechanic to have one's car checked, paying the mechanic for the tests, and then having the mechanic tell you that if you want copies of the test results, or his opinion of what is wrong with your car you'll have to pay an extra $222.
I can understand a doctor charging a nominal fee for the time it might take to have the records photocopied or for the cover letter (hospitals typically charge between $15 and $35 for this service, and it takes much more time for the hospital to locate all the records of one patient, than it would for a private physician, since hospital records are often in several locations throughout the hospital), but the $222 fee is certainly well out of line. Also, I would think it fair that any record that would be sent to third party sources, such as courts, lawyers, insurance companies, etc. should also be provided to the patient to review for accuracy. Anyone can see and correct their confidential financial credit rating, so why not their medical record?
Lastly, I seriously question the policy of not allowing a patient a copy of their medical record, including lab test results, diagnosis and prognosis. In this mobile society, people often change doctors and locations, and medical records are often not retained beyond a few years. With the emphasis on medical history as a diagnostic tool, with slow developing environmental and occupational illnesses, with viruses which do not manifest for up to ten years, retention and access to medical record is becoming more and more important to the health of the patient. I am sure many less misdiagnoses would occur if doctors had better access to longer term medical histories.
The importance of record retention is becoming increasingly apparent. This is important in a number of ways. It is important in tracing the pattern of a single individual's illness from the time when the first symptoms appear and to show how it develops. It is important for being able to trace genetic disease.
Last fall, we had the very interesting story of the Attorney General for Oregon, David Frohnmayer whose two daughters suffer from Franconi's anaemia. Mr. Frohnmayer brought them to a small town in Nova Scotia, Musquodoboit Valley, to try to contact relatives who would have the bone marrow that might be compatible for a bone marrow transplant. It is this type of genetic tracing that can become extremely important.
Again, it is important for us to know of what disease did my grandfather died, and what is the pattern of heart disease, cancer or diabetes in my family. Individuals could find information like that extremely helpful in dealing with their own health.
It is also important for the statistical studies of disease. For example, we have a great many industrial diseases. It might be helpful if we had access to the medical records of workers in bleach plants in the pulp mills across Canada to see how that impacts upon their health. Or we could look at the way in
Patients' Rights
which anti-sapstain application in lumber mills has affected health.
Statistical studies of disease are becoming increasingly important. We just have to look at the effects on children who grow up in families where there is a great deal of heavy smoking; or we can look at the effects of children who live on streets where there are heavy traffic patterns and lead impacts on the environment. There are any number of issues in which environmental concerns that have important impacts upon an individual's health could be examined statistically if these records were available.
There are those who when they hear of this problem of retention of records talk about the cost. I think that we have to balance the cost of retaining these records against the cost of having to repeat tests. We have to balance the cost of retaining records against the value of having access to knowledge that can help to reduce costly disease.
The amazing thing about this situation is that records are not being kept now. We made inquiries of the different provinces in this regard. It is astounding that there is absolutely no pattern across the country as to how long the different provinces keep records.
Newfoundland agrees that retention is worth while, but has no regulations in that regard. Prince Edward Island keeps records for 50 years, if microfilmed, 20 years following discharge or five years following death. Nova Scotia keeps records for seven years, and New Brunswick for 21 years. Quebec keeps records for five years and Ontario for ten years, and this is under review. Manitoba keeps records for 30 years. Saskatchewan is aware of the growing concern and cited cost as a problem. Alberta keeps records for ten years, and British Columbia for six years. The Yukon keeps records for 25 years, while the Northwest Territories understands the benefits of record retention but has no regulations.
In other words, in the whole field of provincial regulations in what other area would we find such a complete hodge-podge where there is absolutely no pattern whatsoever, no rhyme or reason? There is an important role here for the Minister to play. Unfortunately, when I wrote to the Minister he replied that this is under the responsibility of the provinces and territories. We know that. Fie stated: "Thus, it is now up to my provincial/territorial counterparts to bring the matter up for discussion. As I have stated, I will be pleased to respond to any issues or any questions they may wish to raise in this regard." In other words, the federal Government has not indicated that it is willing to take any initiative, in bringing the different provinces together on this issue but that it would be happy to discuss it if one of the provinces chose to raise it.
That is not a good enough response to a serious problem. It is a national problem, not simply a provincial one although health falls under a provincial jurisdiction. People move from one province to another. They move from Prince Edward Island to British Columbia and from Saskatchewan to the Northwest Territories and back to Quebec and so on.

June 2, 1988
Patients' Rights
There is a need for a national initiative and a national coordination. In addition to co-ordination the federal Government probably has a role to play in providing financial help to make this possible. It also has a role in terms of providing storage and access facilities for records after a certain period of time when it would be difficult for hospitals or individual doctors to retain them.
The modern methods of storage, retrieval and transmittal of information encourage this kind of centralized facility. Whenever we talk about centralized storage of personal records and centralized retrieval we pose some problems with regard to civil liberties. Certainly, that is true with medical records.
This is a sensitive area. Perhaps it is one of the areas that the committee should be studying. However, I suggest that the centralization of medical records does not pose a more serious question for civil liberties than does the centralized storage of income tax records and other kinds of sensitive information.
The committee should look at the experiment of some United States insurance companies which give their clients a medical record card which is kept up to date by coded material of test results and doctors' records. This card remains with the patient so that if they change doctors of if they move from one location to another their medical records go with them.
There are possibilities here. In the 20th century and the 21st century, which will soon be upon us, we have to have access to medical records in a way that our present regulations give us absolutely no guarantee of happening. I urge all Members to think about this matter. I hope that they will agree that it is important. I hope that they will agree that it is desirable that there be some national system of retaining records, that there be a recognition of the rights of patients to have access to their own records, and that they will accept this motion.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   HEALTH SUGGESTED DEVELOPMENT OF POLICIES ON PATIENTS' RIGHTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, recently, the Hon. Member for Cowichan-Mala-hat-The Islands (Mr. Manly) asked the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) to take steps to provide for a uniform policy across this country on the preservation of, and access to, medical files.
Mr. Speaker, as you know, under the Canada Health Act all matters connected with medical or hospital files necessarily come under provincial jurisdiction, as do municipal files, for instance. Consequently, until the provincial ministers express an interest in the matter, the Minister of National Health and Welfare of Canada cannot take steps to introduce legislation to that effect. Although in most cases, access to such documents is provided without any problems, free of charge, the fact remains that this Government is sympathetic to the difficulties encountered by some Canadians when they try to obtain access to their medical files.
Mr. Speaker, that is why our colleague, the Minister of National Health and Welfare, is seriously considering the possibility of initiating consultations and talks with the provinces and a number of national health organizations, in order to reach a consensus on legislation concerning medical files, whether the files are kept by health professionals or by a hospital.
For instance, the matter could be submitted to the Advisory Committee on Institutional and Medical Services, whose next meeting will be held in November 1988. Mr. Speaker, as you know, the terms of reference of this Committee are to consider and discuss, at the interprovincial and federal-provincial levels, matters of interest or mutual concern relating to health services or institutional medical services, and include preparing recommendations as appropriate. Matters of interest or mutual concern may be generally understood to include any matter relating to medical files Committee members may decide to discuss.
For your information, Mr. Speaker, the Committee's membership includes senior public servants representing each of the provincial and territorial Governments and the federal Government. If the Committee should express the need for such a policy, the Minister of National Health and Welfare of Canada would be willing to act in such a way as to encourage the creation of uniform policies across this country for the preservation of and access to medical files.
Mr. Speaker, I repeat that this is a matter that falls under provincial jurisdiction. I also wish to mention what has been done by certain provinces to deal with this problem. For instance, in 1984, the Province of Quebec adopted Bill 65 and created the Information Access Commission. Under the legislation, everyone is guaranteed the basic right to access to his own medical files. In Ontario, however, attempts to introduce amendments with the same purpose in mind were unsuccessful. That was the case in 1980, when the Province made an indepth study of this question, as reported by the Krever Commission.
On October 15, 1987, the federal Government tabled a document entitled: Access and Privacy: The Steps Ahead, its response to the Standing Committee's report on access to information and privacy protection.
Mr. Speaker, the Government of Canada recognizes the fact that Canadians must have access to a wide range of information, including personal information. However, it is also absolutely necessary to protect the vital interests of Canadian citizens, so that the right balance is struck between the two. The Access to Information Act guarantees the public's right to information. By definition, this includes all medical information.
Mr. Speaker, it also means that the medical files of over two million Canadians which are now the property of the Minister of National Health and Welfare of Canada, are available to them without charge, except for the cost of photocopying the files.
June 2, 1988

In concluding, Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank the Hon. Member for Cowichan-Malahat-The Islands for raising this very important issue.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to start by congratulating the Hon. Member for Cowichan-Malahat-The Islands (Mr. Manly) on his decision to bring this motion to the attention of the House. This is a very important matter.
In his motion, the Hon. Member says:
... the government should consider the advisability of participating with the provinces in the consideration and development of policies in the field of patients' rights, including the right of patients to have access to their files ...
He goes on to recommend that doctors and hospitals have the obligation to keep patients' records for at least fifty years, and to encourage the enactment of provincial legislation on such matters.
Mr. Speaker, I agree that this is not a federal matter as such. However, I think this House has the right to express its common wish and desire to see the provinces establish a system, as they see fit, that would provide for a uniform policy across this country with respect to the disclosure and preservation of patients' records.
Mr. Speaker, the Privacy Commissioner's Annual Report for 1984 mentioned a complaint about a medical report. This is what it says:
An Ontario man, refused a disability pension under the Canada Pension Plan, complained to the Privacy Commissioner that he was denied access to the report which generated the refusal. The complainant had authorized Health and Welfare Canada to obtain proof of his disability from the Workers' Compensation Board. The Commission provided the report but refused to give it to the applicant when he was refused a pension.
This is an example of a Canadian who was denied access to his own medical record.
Mr. Speaker, I already had the honour and privilege to sit in the Ontario Legislative Assembly, as the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Jelinek) pointed out earlier today in this House, and as an MPP, I often had to defend cases where work accidents were overlooked, where workers had been injured on the job or in the workplace. And many times I had to call doctors and hospitals to get medical reports for my constituents from them.
Interestingly enough, it was often the constituent who went to the hospital for his or her medical record and was refused. If the MPP called, he was given the file. One wonders why! In many cases, the constituent could have defended his own case for worker's compensation if he had had access to the document in question. And I find it quite wrong that the patient should be refused what the MPP could obtain. Of course, when I as MPP had the file, we both got together around a table, the constituent and I-and I am sure that most MPPs still do-to share the information in order to better defend the accident victim's claim.
Patients' Rights
It is sometimes hard to understand why there is that reluctance on the part of the medical profession to make available to patients their medical records.
I have a newspaper article written by Mr. Arthur Schafer, the Director of the Centre for Professional and Applied Ethics at the University of Manitoba. Mr. Schafer refers to an article from The New England Journal of Medicine in which an American doctor says that there is sometimes a reluctance on the part of the medical profession to make medical records available because patients could potentially find out about mistakes made by doctors. The article reads in part:
Dr. Hilfiker recounts, for example, how he relied upon negative results produced by the standard pregnancy test when deciding to perform a dilation in curettage-on one of his patients. Had he ordered an ultrasound examination before he scraped out her uterus, he would have discovered that she had a viable pregnancy. He relied too heavily upon one kind of test, and was insufficiently skillful in determining the size of the uterus by pelvic examination. The result of this error: "Nothing can obscure the hard reality:
I... killed their baby."
That also gives the doctor's position on abortion, one with which I concur. However, the point I am making is that it is obvious that in a case like this the doctor would not have had much to gain by giving that information to the patient.
I do not want to accuse all doctors of making it difficult for medical information or medical reports to reach patients for similar reasons, but it is, nevertheless, the view of the author of this article that there are occasions on which the medical profession is hesitant to provide information because the information in question could be detrimental to the practitioner.
I suppose there are other reasons for this as well. Sometimes medical practitioners make notes in the file to which a patient reading the note would take offence. There are occasions, of course, on which a patient may have a disease, the news of which must be broken to the patient in a specific manner.
If a patient is terminally ill the doctor may have to inform the patient of this in such a manner as to ensure that the patient will not go into an immediate depression or some other medical condition. Physicians know how to break such news although I would not, obviously. If the patient requested his or her file that very day and it was provided, the patient could be negatively affected I suppose. Therefore, I recognize that there are occasions on which a physician would have to use proper judgment and not provide information immediately.
When defending a worker at the Workers' Compensation Board I ran across a case in which a medical practitioner had indicated in the file that the claimant's difficulty in readjusting to the workforce was due to the fact that he was, in the view of the practitioner, somewhat deficient in terms of his mental ability. I imagine that had the claimant seen that, he would not have been too happy with the physician who did not have specific training in that field. This was a general practitioner,

June 2, 1988
Patients' Rights
not someone who had done a thorough mental examination of the patient. Obviously, had the patient seen that, he would have been offended by the doctor describing him as suffering from mental retardation, which I believe was the actual term used in the medical note in that file.
Therefore, I realize there are circumstances which could cause medical practitioners to be reticent to have patients view their files. However, in my opinion that is not generally an excuse for not providing that information to the patient. If it is the file of the patient, in my opinion it is the patient's file.
The medical profession, together with the provinces, could probably adopt an ethical way of releasing the document. If it is sensitive at a particular time a specific delay may be invoked in certain cases for certain medical reasons, but simply to refuse to give it out either to protect the physician or to cause less expense for the physician or hospital is not satisfactory.
Having defended workers at compensation hearings in the past I know it is difficult to get that information, or at least it was in the days when I was a member of the Ontario Legislature. It was not impossible, but it was difficult, and, in my opinion, unnecessarily so.
It is my opinion that if we had a uniform system across the country established by the provinces, of course, perhaps with input and assistance by the federal Government, such a system would be helpful to injured workers and other people needing access to their medical files for whatever reason.
I am pleased to support this initiative. I do not want it to be interpreted that we intend to impose this on the provinces. That is certainly not the way I read the motion. The motion does not propose to impose it on anyone. It proposes a process of consultation and assistance to the provinces in establishing this. That is the way I see it as well. Given that that is the tone of the motion as I read it, I am happy to support it.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   HEALTH SUGGESTED DEVELOPMENT OF POLICIES ON PATIENTS' RIGHTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would certainly like to congratulate the Hon. Member for Cowichan-Malahat-The Islands (Mr. Manly) for bringing this matter to the attention of the House this afternoon. It is a very interesting and important matter and although, as the Member correctly points out in the motion, most of that with which we are dealing lies within provincial or territorial jurisdiction, it is quite properly a matter for debate in this House.
I notice that the motion is really divided into two parts, the first deals with patients' rights in general, and the second deals with access to records and a proposed standardized period of retention of records of some 50 years.
I want to address most of my remarks to the first part of the motion, one that has not really been dealt with yet. When one enters a hospital, a person undergoes a radical change in status. When you are on the outside, you are very much in control of your own affairs. You do what you want to do and
when you want to do it. Once a person passes through hospital doors and is admitted, life is much different. When you are on the inside you are told when to go to sleep, when to get up, what you have to eat, when you have to eat it, what drugs you have to take and what kind of needles have to be stuck into you. It is an entirely different social situation in which you find yourself.
It has never really happened to me, but I have studied other people who have had the experience. The situation must be pretty difficult to take. Most of us do and accept it because we know that it is in our own best interests. The tendency in a hospital is to be treated like a thing or a number. Perhaps it is more akin to being treated as a child rather than an adult. But the situation is almost unavoidable. Hospital personnel try very hard and most, I am sure, do the best they possibly can to be as humane as possible to patients, but there will always be certain exceptions.
I do not know whether we can legislate in this area. We can obviously legislate things such as criminal negligence and so on, but perhaps what each and every hospital should adopt is some form of a patients' bill of rights, something that can become part of a particular hospital's policy, something with which the administration of a hospital could make sure that its staff and physicians are familiar and something the staff can keep foremost in their minds when dealing with patients. Maybe this bill of rights could be posted in a conspicuous place in several locations around a hospital for the benefit of the staff and the patients. Maybe when an accreditation committee makes its rounds periodically the presence or absence of a patients' bill of rights should be something which it could take into account when making examinations. Included in a bill of rights could be a mechanism to deal with any complaints and any recommendations patients may have.
One of the problems that we have in medicine today-it is one of the prices we pay for what is generally a good system of socialized medicine in Canada-is that you lose that "client" relationship between a patient and a doctor or a patient and a hospital because someone else is paying the bill. Sometimes you get the impression that hospitals may not be quite as nice to a patient as they should be because they know it is not the patient who is paying the bill but a third party.
The second part of the motion deals with medical records. I agree wholeheartedly with the position taken by the proposer. I have never been able to understand the reluctance to allow people to see their own medical records. It seems to me that it is an elementary right that should be available to anyone. I do not agree with the argument sometimes used that medical records are couched in technical language and people are not able to understand them. You can get legal records about yourself, but most people have difficulty reading those.
I remember many years ago trying in a provincial House to amend the law to give people access to medical records made as a result of examinations by workers' compensation physicians. We were unable to do that. I could not then and cannot
June 2, 1988

now think of any reason why somebody should be refused access to records made by workers' compensation physicians. It is interesting to note that those people who opposed my proposal at that time were people generally of a socialistic leaning. I am unable to understand that either. Surely when we have dealt with access to information in general terms and we have passed access to information legislation in this House, that access should be equally applicable to medical records. Of course, the other side of the coin is privacy.
Medical records should, of course, be private. You have something of a built-in conflict between the two as we have between the Access to Information Act and the Privacy Act. One might want to make some kind of distinction between medical records on the one hand and what might be described as doctors' notes on the other. I know that doctors might be reluctant to have made available hand-scribbled notes which they have made on the spur of the moment. Similarly, a Member of Parliament would have no objection to giving anybody a copy of any letter that he or she has ever written, but I do not know that I would want to hand out transcripts of notes or doodles that I have made when answering the telephone. I can understand the reluctance of certain physicians to hand out information. It might very often be wanted in connection with a malpractice suit or something like that. It seems that very often medical records are easily interchangeable between physicians and government Departments and agencies thereof, such as workers' compensation boards, and this is done with considerable ease. The only people who are not able to get in on this and not able to get copies of records are those most intimately involved, namely the patient.
With respect to the proposed 50 years suggested time for retention of records, at first blush that seems a little bit long. Fifty years is certainly longer than the working career of most physicians. In the days before the computer, if we had insisted on the retention of records for 50 years, we would have used up all doctors' offices and surgeries for the storage of paper in no time flat. With the coming of the computer it might make longer term retention a lot simpler. Certainly, as the Hon. Member pointed out, it would be very useful for medical research to have statistical studies to look into hereditary type diseases.
There is a wide variety of practices from one jurisdiction to another. Surely we can work toward a more standardized system right across Canada. I am advised of the existence of a committee called the Federal-Provincial Advisory Committee on Institutional Medical Services, which is a creature of the Conference of Deputy Ministers of Health. It would seem to me to make a good deal of sense, and that committee may have done so in the past, for that committee to take this matter under study so that eventually we could come up with a systematic national system.
Thank you very much, Mr. Speaker, for your kind attention, and once again I thank the Hon. Member for Cowichan-
Patients' Rights
Malahat-The Islands for bringing to the attention of this Chamber such an interesting topic.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   HEALTH SUGGESTED DEVELOPMENT OF POLICIES ON PATIENTS' RIGHTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I too am very pleased to rise today in strong support of the motion of my colleague, the Hon. Member for Cowichan- Malahat-The Islands (Mr. Manly). It is an interesting and quite an important proposal. It is nice to know that Members on all sides of the House support it.
The motion reads:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of participating with the provinces in the consideration and development of policies in the field of patients' rights, including the right of patients to have access to their files and the obligation for doctors and hospitals to keep patients' records for at least fifty years, and to encourage the enactment of provincial legislation on such matters.
I know, after talking to the Hon. Member and looking at some of his background materials, that his preparation for this motion has been very interesting. He has contacted all the different provinces and has documented the kind of recording procedures that exist at this time. I know that the Hon. Member referred to this in his remarks.
At the present time, there is no federal legislation which regulates the length of time medical records must be retained, nor is there any legislation requiring doctors or hospitals to release medical records or test results to patients. The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) has indicated that such legislation and regulation is in the provincial jurisdiction and it is up to his provincial territorial counterparts to bring the matter up for discussion. I rather question this position, because under the principle of medicare, the federal Government is supposed to ensure a system that is universal, with universal access and portability among provinces.
We are told that if the provinces do bring this matter up for discussion, the Minister has said that he would be pleased to respond to any issues or questions they may wish to raise in this regard. I am pleased that my colleague has been in touch with the provinces, and I hope that this will stimulate some action on the part of provincial Ministers to put this on a common agenda with the Minister of National Health and Welfare.
As is the case when matters lie within provincial jurisdiction, the provinces and territories tend to respond in different ways with different approaches. On the matter of the retention of medical records, responses have varied from that of Prince Edward Island, which keeps them for 50 years if microfilmed, for 20 years following discharge or for five years following death, to those of Saskatchewan and the Northwest Territories which have no regulation to keep them at all. That seems to be a very strange policy. Of course, other provinces have varying regulations.
The other part of the problem lies with the fact that patients have no rights of access to their own medical records. I agree with the previous speaker who said that we should have a statement of patients' rights to which the medical profession

June 2, 1988
Patients' Rights
and hospitals should adhere. At this time, neither doctors nor hospitals are under any obligation to share medical files with patients, and whether or not they do so is entirely up to their own judgment.
Further to the difficulties of obtaining patients' files, the cost of obtaining copies of files is also discretionary to the doctor. The B.C. Medical Association, for instance, suggests that there should be a charge of S222 for this, plus photocopying fees. This seems to be ridiculous since we do have a medicare plan which surely should be able to cover such expenses.

Double billing, as my colleague has said, quite correctly.
The Hon. Member for Cowichan-Malahat-The Islands has written to all the provincial Ministers of Health urging them to initiate discussions with the federal Minister of Health so that patients' rights will be met in a consistent manner across Canada. This is a basic principle of medicare. The Hon. Member wrote them in October of last year, and unfortunately there has been no action other than the supplying of the information to which we both referred.
I strongly concur with my colleague that it has become incumbent upon the federal Minister of Health to take the initiative to put this matter before the provinces for discussion. This Minister, repeatedly, on many different issues, has preferred to take a laissez-faire approach, sometimes deliberate and perhaps sometimes through neglect, when he should have been taking a leadership role. He has the right and the obligation to assume a leadership role in ensuring that there is a good quality of medical records, and that relates to a good quality of medical procedures across Canada.
There are some very good reasons for keeping good medical records and for providing fair and equitable access to them for all Canadians in a standardized way. Obtaining accurate medical histories is essential to moving our health care system away from its focus on curative methods only toward a more preventive approach. The Minister of National Health and Welfare himself has endorsed this direction for Canada's health care system in his document Achieving Health for All: A Framework for Health Protection.
As we know, some conditions and diseases are hereditary or genetic. Access to medical records would allow the transfer of correct information to offspring and other relatives. It also provides data for research into genetic diseases.
I understand that Canada already has better access to records for research purposes in some instances than countries which do not have a public medicare system, and that is very good. Certainly, however, longer and more consistent case histories that cover a period of a family's history would be very valuable, not only to the patient involved but to medical researchers.
Canadians are very mobile. We move between provinces and territories all the time. This is another reason for such a system, and other colleagues have mentioned this as well.
In the case of liability suits and legal matters, access to medical records can be essential to victims. An example of this is the harm done to the victims by the Daikon Shield or Thalidomide. As well, women whose mothers took the chemical DES may be subject to developing cancer.
There are many reasons for adopting this motion, and I have many more which I do not have time to present. In view of the time limits with which we are faced, I would like to move:
That this motion be accepted by the House.
I would like as well to call for a vote on this matter.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to be able to speak on this motion. The reality is that our time is expiring, but I would still like to say a couple of words.
As the motion before the House suggests, one important aspect of the broader issue of patients' rights relates to the patients' access to medical records. The federal Government is currently involved with native and inmate health care. However, any consideration of access to medical records at the federal level would not be complete without reference to the Privacy Act. The Privacy Act was given Royal Assent on July 7, 1982, and was proclaimed into force on July 1, 1983. The purpose of the Privacy Act is set out in Section 2 as follows:
The purpose of this Act is to extend the present laws of Canada that protect
the privacy of individuals with respect to personal information about
themselves held by a government institution and that provide individuals with
a right of access to such information.
As this important provision suggests, the Act has two basic objectives. First, it is intended to protect an individual's privacy. Second, it is intended to provide individuals with a right of access to information about themselves which is under the control of government institutions. Both these objectives are relevant to any discussion of patients' rights.
The focus of the Privacy Act is personal information. This term is defined by the Act to mean information about an identifiable individual that is recorded in any form including information relating to the medical history of the individual. Thus, it seems clear that a patient's medical records would fall within this definition as long as the patient could be identified therefrom.

HEALTH-PULP MILL OUTFALLS-DIOXIN LEVELS IN CRABS/EXAMPLE SET BY SWEDISH PULP MILLS.

Mr. Speaker, on May 17 I raised with the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) the question of dioxin testing around pulp mills in Canada, particularly in British Columbia. As you know, dioxins are the most dangerous substances known to humanity. They do not break down when they are released into the environment. Rather, they accumulate. Therefore, this is an extremely important question concerning our health.
In the last number of years we have become aware of the fact that our pulp mills produce dioxins. Therefore, this testing process was very important. As a result, the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan), the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. Siddon), and the Minister of National Health and Welfare released a press statement saying that there is no problem, nothing to worry about. I quote from the statement:
The results of analyses of fish samples in these surveys have been evaluated by Health and Welfare officials. They have indicated that the levels of dioxins and furans found in the edible portions of fish samples are not considered to pose a health hazard to consumers.
Relatively higher levels of dioxins and furans have been identified in a few samples of prawns and crabs, particularly in the digestive gland (hepatopan-creas) of dungeness crabs, taken near pulp mills in Port Mellon, Woodfibre and Prince Rupert, British Columbia.
Health and Welfare has recommended that further samples from these three sites be analysed to assess whether these recent findings are representative.
The elevated levels of dioxins and furans found in the digestive gland of crabs are not unexpected as this organ concentrates ingested materials including contaminants such as dioxins and furans. Since this portion of the crab is not normally eaten, the levels found do not pose a hazard with respect to consumption of the edible portion of crabs.
Following that statement we had headlines such as "Pulp Mills Said No Threat To Fish Eaters", and "Dioxin In Fish No Threat: Govt. Test" and "Level Of Dioxin In Fish No Threat, Siddon Says". I think those headlines and the press release are belied by the facts released along with the press statement.
Background information points out that of three samples of oysters taken near Crofton, there were findings of 31, 12, and 14 parts per trillion respectively of dioxin in those three samples. There is a tolerance threshold of 20 parts per trillion. Therefore, one out of those three was much above that 20 part per trillion threshold, with 31 parts per trillion. They point out that there is no problem there because the area is already closed because of other forms of pollution. However, the fact is
Adjournment Debate
that the oysters there are at risk and people who eat them as they are, are also at risk.
Then they talk about crab hepatopancreas. Residues of 2, 3, 7, 8-TCDD, that is dioxin, in the crab hepatopancreas from several different areas ranged up to 100 parts per trillion. We must recall that 20 parts per trillion is the tolerance level. However, three samples, one each from Port Mellon, Wood-fibre, and Prince Rupert contained 662, 356 and 487 parts per trillion 2, 3, 7, 8-TCDD respectively.
The other less toxic dioxic congeners ranged from non detectable to 1,514 parts per trillion in crab hepatopancreas with the exception of the three samples from the above noted sites where a maximum level of 4,682 parts per trillion was observed. Residues of 2, 3, 7, 8-TCDF ranged from non detectable to 2,605 parts per trillion, except in the case of the three samples for Port Mellon, Woodfibre and Prince Rupert where residues of 2, 3, 7, 8-TCDF ranged from 18,890 parts per trillion to 24,968 parts per trillion.
That is a frightening statistic. First, we do not know what we are talking about. The Government does not have any level of equivalency for these other toxins to equate it with dioxin. Yet there are some very high levels.
The Government does not explain what the equivalency levels are because it does not have equivalency levels established. It has said that the hepatopancreas is not normally eaten, but the fact is that it is considered a delicacy by some people.
The serious nature of this issue is shown by a study of the great blue heron colony near Crofton which forages on the flats near the pulp mill. Last year, of 57 nests, not a single egg hatched. When they studied the residue of the eggs, they found that there had been a threefold increase in the level of dioxins in 1987 from 1986. This is a serious problem, and the headlines that say there is nothing to worry about do a disservice to Canadians.
The Government should take action in four areas. It should forbid all fishing in the immediate area of pulp mill outflows. There should be more rigid monitoring and enforcement of pollution control. Twenty-one out of 22 pulp mills in British Columbia are in violation of federal pollution standards but nothing was done about it.
The Government should bring in tough new regulations that will force pulp mills to reduce dioxin levels as is done in Sweden and West Germany where those levels have been cut by 80 per cent. Finally, it should encourage the production and consumption of unbleached and semi-bleached pulp products, rather than continuing this fetish with totally bleached white products that are doing us and the environment great damage.

speakeroldname: Mr. Pat Binns (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Fisheries and Oceans):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Cowichan-Malahat-The Islands (Mr. Manly) must be

June 2, 1988
Adjournment Debate
congratulated for continuing in his interest in this very important environmental area with respect to the fishing industry and shellfish in particular. The class of chemical substances known as dioxins has been described in the media and elsewhere as being the most toxic chemicals known to man. Certainly, this Government does not in any way take away from that recognition. Consequently, any reports of dioxins being present in the environment, and particularly in the food supply, understandably evoke a great deal of concern in all of us and in the Government in particular.
I want to assure the Elouse that the Government is not only concerned about dioxins and toxic chemicals in mollusks and fish in general. I believe Canada has the safest fish products anywhere in the world reaching the market-place. For instance, in Atlantic Canada every body of water used for harvesting of mollusks and other shellfish is being tested on a regular basis to ensure that the products are safe for consumption. There is a very rigorous examination and standard to ensure that the fish consumers are eating are safe. As I indicated, it is the safest food we have available to us at the present time.
However, it is important to know some facts about these substances before arriving at any conclusions about the possible hazards associated with their presence in fish and shellfish. The term "dioxin", for example, does not refer to one compound but rather to a whole family of 75 related chemical compounds. These 75 compounds are also often associated with another family or organochlorine compounds known as furans. There are an additional 135 related, yet individual, compounds in the furan family.
One might question the significance of all of this to the assessment of dioxins and furans in fish and shellfish with respect to any potential hazard to the health of the consumer. Well, Mr. Speaker, the fact is that based on the available information relating to these compounds, it is known that the toxicity of the individual members of the dioxin and furan family varies significantly. The most toxic is 2,3,7. 8-TCDD, or 2,3,7, 8-Tetrachlorodibenzo-para-dioxin for which a limit has been established under the Canadian Food and Drug Regulations of 20 parts per trillion in fish. The other dioxin and furan isomers have not yet been studied as intensively as 2,3,7, 8-TDCC, but on the basis of the available data they are considered relatively less toxic.
The reported levels of up to 25 parts per billion of these substances in shellfish relate to levels of individual furans in the digestive glands of crabs from one specific location. Such levels in the digestive glands of scavengers like crabs, taken near a waste disposal effluent pipe, are not unexpected since this organ concentrates many types of ingested substances. Furthermore, Mr. Speaker, while there have been anecdotal reports of consumption of the viscera of crab, consultations with officials in the British Columbia Ministry of Health have not confirmed these reports. Clearly, it is in everyone's best interest to minimize exposure to toxic chemicals such as dioxins and furans. But let us proceed in a rational and orderly
fashion based on sound information so that we can ensure that consumer products are safe for the fishery.
UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-CANADA PACKERS-CLOSURE OF WINNIPEG PLANT-WORKERS' UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE BENEFITS/DIFFERENCE IN TREATMENT OF SALARIED EMPLOYEES AND WAGE EARNERS

Mr. Speaker, I rise tonight on an issue of fairness. When I raised this issue in the House on March 30, the then Minister of Employment and Immigration agreed that the problem was serious enough to warrant a very thorough investigation. I am talking about the closure of the Canada Packers Plant in Winnipeg.
In December of 1986, Canada Packers announced that its plant would be closing and 660 workers in the Winnipeg plant would lose their jobs by early 1988. In April 1987, a collective agreement was amended to provide allocation of separation payments to a one week period following the closure.
Then, on April 5, 1987, the unemployment insurance regulations changed to require that separation payments be considered earnings as per the regular week's salary, regardless of collective agreements. This would delay unemployment insurance claims by the number of weeks represented by severance pay earnings.
The reality of the situation is one-half the workers who were laid off on April 10, 1987, received their severance pay which was seen to be one week's pay. They were allowed to collect their unemployment insurance.
This year what has happened is that the rest of the plant closed. Over 300 workers were laid off. They were told that because it was after the unemployment insurance amendments had taken effect that they would not receive their severance pay as representative of one week but that it would be taken as a week for each week of salary earned. Unfortunately, it was older workers who were laid off latterly. We know it takes older workers longer to get back into the workforce. We also know that there was a number of older workers who have not been able to get back into the workforce. They are now seen as people who are not participating.
We have to take into account as well that these older workers have depended on their Canada Pension and retirement plans for their existence. Certainly, in many cases it is not a very lucrative existence after the age of 65. All the years that they do not pay into these plans is depleting them of what they will receive at age 65. The fact is that they have had to spend their severance pay at a time which could have been included as part of a retirement plan. They are now excluded from doing that.
To make the matter even more unfair, what has happened is that when the doors of the plant were closed, the salaried workers were exempted. These are workers who very often receive a much more generous settlement for all sorts of
June 2, 1988

reasons, such as their salary or their status in the company. They were allowed to look at their severance pay as one week of pay after which they could collect unemployment insurance.
This gross unfairness is something that even the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) addressed in Winnipeg. He said he was very concerned about it and that he wanted to look into it. He did look into it. He reviewed the situation when he was in Manitoba.
Strange as it may seem, after the Manitoba election the Prime Minister said that there was no justification for them to have an exemption. Surely there is a justification. Both groups of workers were working in the same plant. They knew at the same time that the plant would close. To add insult to injury, one group of workers which left the plant on the very same day had an exemption made for them. We are not only talking about a very unjust kind of policy. We are talking about a Government which promised to do something for older workers.
The Government announced in 1986 that it would do something for older workers. It still has not done anything. It announced that $125 million would be made available. Yet it has not implemented anything.
In my riding of Hamilton Mountain there are many older workers who have not been able to get back into the workforce. Those between the ages of 50 and 65 are certainly looking at a much reduced income in terms of pension. Over and above that they are having a very difficult time trying to find employment.
It is very clear to me, and I do not know why it is complicated for the Government, that this is a very unfair situation. We are talking about people from the very same plant who work for the same number of years and in many cases who were friends. Very often the ones who are being deprived are ones who taught others their skills. It seems clear to me that the Government should make an exception in this case and rectify the injustice which has gone on. Not only would an injustice be rectified but a great deal of comfort would be given to families which are suffering very much at this time.

speakeroldname: Mr. Benno Friesen (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Ms. McDougall) I am pleased to respond to the Hon. Member for Hamilton Mountain (Ms. Dewar).
First, I want to say that I was disappointed in the way she framed her question on March 30, a question which she ended by stating that this was a case of discrimination. That is probably the easiest accusation to throw around nowadays. It does not matter what level of Government or what agency wants to provide help, benefit, or a program for any group of citizens deemed to require help. The group that is just beyond the fringe of receiving that benefit cries discrimination. It is unfortunate that the Hon. Member used that word. The Act
Adjournment Debate
and the manner in which the Act has been applied is not discriminatory.
The Hon. Member comes from a rich experience of city administration and now represents a riding which is very active in union work, and union and collective agreements. It is not correct for the Hon. Member to suggest that there is a difference between salaried employees and hourly paid employed employees. If she asked a second or third question about the problem about the question she would know that it has nothing to do with whether or not they are salaried or paid by the hour, but it has everything to do with when the collective agreement was arrived at.
They are all the same.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
speechtext:
No, they are not. The collective agreement for the salaried people was pre-1985. The collective agreement for the hourly workers, at least one part of it, came into force in June, 1987. That triggers an entirely different response on the basis of the Act. If the Act is applied fairly and legally for both groups, one cannot say that it is discriminatory. At the time the collective agreement was arrived at, the Act was already in force, and the workers knew that.
I wish to say to the Hon. Member that I understand exactly what she means when she talks about the distress, particularly of older workers who have a difficult time finding employment again, especially if they have been in that one location for 30 years and have perhaps not done any other type of work since they were teenagers. It is not easy. It is very difficult.
The other factor not included by the Hon. Member is when one is dealing with a collective agreement, one of the most important ingredients is seniority. I know that the Hon. Member would not want anybody to infringe on the seniority rights of the employees. When the first group of employees became unemployed or were laid off, naturally it was those who had not worked so long at the plant. Those who stayed on for another few months were the senior members.
In this case, it worked to their disadvantage in terms of reemployment. It probably would not have made much difference in terms of the space between the two periods of lay-offs. But in this case, seniority worked against the senior workers. I think the Hon. Member understands that. She has pointed that out and elaborated correctly in her remarks.
The Hon. Member also pointed out that in the legislation which was adopted in 1985 there was a factor which was used by the labour management people to balloon all of the severance pay into one week, thereby making the unemployment insurance provisions trigger more quickly. This was deemed to be an avoidance or circumventing the effect of the UI regulations. The Government is bound by that. It was changed by an amendment passed on April 5, 1987, and that amendment was passed before the next collective agreement came into force.
